title: Robust and Efficient AI Frameworks for Scalable Material Design and Property Prediction
summary:
This thesis develops robust and efficient AI frameworks for accelerating crystalline materials discovery by addressing both major stages of the materials-design pipeline: crystal property prediction and crystal structure generation. Motivated by the high computational cost of Density Functional Theory (DFT) and the limited availability of labeled materials data, the thesis explores graph representation learning, pretraining, multimodal learning, and generative modeling for scalable materials design.
  For property prediction, the thesis first introduces CrysXPP, which learns transferable crystal representations through unsupervised graph autoencoding, reducing dependence on large property-labeled datasets. It then proposes CrysGNN, a large-scale self-supervised graph pretraining framework that captures atomic connectivity, chemical attributes, and global structural information and transfers this knowledge to downstream property predictors through knowledge distillation. CrysMMNet further enriches crystal representations by jointly modeling graph structure and textual descriptions, thereby incorporating both local chemical and global structural knowledge.
  For crystal generation, the thesis introduces TGDMat, a text-guided joint diffusion framework that jointly models lattice parameters, atomic types, and atomic coordinates while incorporating textual structural knowledge during denoising. This enables the generation of more valid and stable periodic materials while also supporting conditional generation from natural-language descriptions.
  Overall, the thesis establishes a unified AI-based framework for data-efficient property prediction and controllable crystal generation, demonstrating how graph learning, multimodal representations, and generative models can reduce computational cost and improve the scalability of materials

AI.tldr: This thesis builds a unified AI framework spanning both stages of the materials-design pipeline—crystal property prediction (CrysXPP, CrysGNN, CrysMMNet) and crystal structure generation (TGDMat)—to enable data-efficient, controllable, and scalable crystalline materials discovery.
AI.motivation: DFT is computationally expensive and property-labeled materials data are scarce, which bottlenecks the materials-design pipeline. The work targets both major stages—property prediction and structure generation—to make materials discovery cheaper and more scalable.
AI.method: For prediction: CrysXPP learns transferable crystal representations via unsupervised graph autoencoding to reduce reliance on labeled data; CrysGNN is a large-scale self-supervised graph pretraining framework encoding atomic connectivity, chemical attributes, and global structure, transferring knowledge to downstream predictors via knowledge distillation; CrysMMNet jointly models graph structure and textual descriptions for multimodal crystal representations. For generation: TGDMat is a text-guided joint diffusion framework that co-models lattice parameters, atomic types, and atomic coordinates with textual structural knowledge injected during denoising.
AI.result: The proposed methods reduce dependence on large property-labeled datasets (CrysXPP, CrysGNN), enrich representations with local chemical and global structural knowledge (CrysMMNet), and generate more valid and stable periodic materials while supporting conditional generation from natural-language descriptions (TGDMat).
AI.conclusion: The thesis establishes a unified AI-based framework for data-efficient property prediction and controllable crystal generation, showing that graph learning, multimodal representations, and generative modeling can cut computational cost and improve the scalability of materials design.

title: Conditions for the Emergence of Spontaneous Phonon Frequency Combs from Anharmonic Potentials
summary: Phononic frequency combs have been demonstrated experimentally and theoretically in the kHz-MHz regime under nonlinear driving; however, their spontaneous formation in the GHz-THz regime remains rare. We investigate the spontaneous formation of frequency combs in van der Waals solid CrGeTe$_3$, where combs of spacing $\sim$2 cm$^{-1}$ were experimentally proposed to occur in a flat phonon mode but are now reported to originate from isotopic distribution. Our spectral energy density calculations using machine-learning-augmented molecular dynamics simulations show comb-like features with reduced spacings of $\sim$0.1 and 0.6 cm$^{-1}$ in the same mode at 50 and 200 K. However, the spacings of the comb-like features are comparable to the phonon linewidth, making precise identification of the frequency comb challenging. From a comprehensive analysis of different modes of CrGeTe$_3$, we identified two conditions to distinctively observe the combs beyond the experimental resolution: (i) an intramolecular or isolated mode with reasonably large third- or higher-order anharmonicity from phonon self-interaction and (ii) limited phonon scattering channels. Our analysis of other van der Waals solids highlighted that these conditions are met for the nearly flat intramolecular $E_{2g}$ and $A_{2u}$ phonon modes of WSe$_2$. The detailed calculations showed the formation of a spontaneous frequency comb with spacings of 1.7 and 0.67 cm$^{-1}$ from coherent superposition of four and five-phonon eigenstates in the $E_{2g}$ and $A_{2u}$ phonon modes, respectively. Available Raman scattering data of the $E_{2g}$ mode in the literature provide preliminary, if not conclusive, evidence of comb formation. Our findings offer a deeper understanding and open avenues for engineering long-lived phononic frequency combs for various practical applications.

AI.tldr: Spontaneous GHz-THz phononic frequency combs are investigated in van der Waals solids; the previously proposed CrGeTe3 combs are attributed to isotopic distribution, and two conditions for distinct comb observation are identified, with WSe2 E2g and A2u modes predicted to host robust combs.
AI.motivation: Phononic frequency combs have been demonstrated in the kHz-MHz regime under nonlinear driving, but spontaneous formation in the GHz-THz regime remains rare. A prior experimental claim of combs in CrGeTe3 is now questioned, motivating a systematic theoretical and computational study of the conditions under which spontaneous phononic combs can be unambiguously resolved.
AI.method: Machine-learning-augmented molecular dynamics simulations are used to compute spectral energy densities for CrGeTe3 and other van der Waals solids. The analysis examines comb-like spectral features, their spacing, and their relation to phonon linewidths, and surveys anharmonicity and phonon scattering channels across different phonon modes.
AI.result: In CrGeTe3, comb-like features with reduced spacings of ~0.1 and 0.6 cm-1 are found in the same flat mode at 50 and 200 K, but the spacings are comparable to the phonon linewidth, precluding precise identification. Two conditions for distinct comb observation are identified: (i) an intramolecular or isolated mode with large third- or higher-order anharmonicity, and (ii) limited phonon scattering channels. These are met for the nearly flat intramolecular E2g and A2u modes of WSe2, where spontaneous combs with spacings of 1.7 and 0.67 cm-1 arise from coherent superposition of four and five-phonon eigenstates, respectively. Existing Raman data for the E2g mode provide preliminary evidence of comb formation.
AI.conclusion: Spontaneous phononic frequency combs in the GHz-THz regime require spectrally resolvable spacings relative to phonon linewidths, which are favored in isolated or intramolecular modes with strong anharmonicity and limited scattering channels. The E2g and A2u modes of WSe2 are promising candidates, and these findings guide the engineering of long-lived phononic frequency combs for practical applications.

title: A Multipolar Approach to Sliding Ferroelectricity
summary: Traditional theoretical treatments of ferroelectricity do not straightforwardly extend to sliding ferroelectrics, which are increasingly-studied layered materials where a switchable electrical polarization is controlled by two-dimensional relative motion of the stacked layers. Therefore, in-depth analyses of the underlying processes which dictate their polarization behavior remain challenging. In this paper, we present a comprehensive approach for identifying the symmetry-adapted microscopic parameters which are responsible for driving the emergence of this polarization. First, we outline our approach, which appeals to group theory arguments and the distortion of Wannier orbital densities to connect macroscopic symmetries to the microscopic electronic distortions which dictate the appearance of ferroelectricity. Then, we illustrate this process by using density functional theory to apply our strategy to honeycomb bilayer systems, including hexagonal boron nitride. In this way, we find that combinations of dipole-like and quadrupole-like distortions of lone pair electron orbitals control electronic reorganization, and by extension, ferroelectricity in such systems.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a group-theory and Wannier-based approach to identify the microscopic symmetry-adapted parameters that drive ferroelectricity in sliding ferroelectrics, applying it to honeycomb bilayers including hexagonal boron nitride via DFT.
AI.motivation: Traditional theoretical treatments of ferroelectricity do not straightforwardly extend to sliding ferroelectrics, where switchable polarization arises from two-dimensional relative motion of stacked layers. In-depth understanding of the underlying processes dictating their polarization behavior remains challenging.
AI.method: The authors present a comprehensive approach combining group theory arguments with analysis of the distortion of Wannier orbital densities, linking macroscopic symmetries to the microscopic electronic distortions that produce ferroelectricity. They apply this strategy using density functional theory (DFT) to honeycomb bilayer systems, including hexagonal boron nitride.
AI.result: The analysis identifies combinations of dipole-like and quadrupole-like distortions of lone pair electron orbitals as the key factor controlling electronic reorganization and, consequently, ferroelectricity in these systems.
AI.conclusion: The proposed group-theory- and Wannier-based framework successfully identifies the symmetry-adapted microscopic parameters underlying sliding ferroelectricity, demonstrating that dipole-like and quadrupole-like orbital distortions govern the effect in honeycomb bilayer systems such as hexagonal boron nitride.

title: Surface chemistry investigation of an additively manufactured Al-Mg-Si-Zr alloy: Studies from experiments and first-principles simulation
summary: The surface chemistry of additively manufactured aluminum alloys plays a critical role in corrosion resistance and joining with external materials. In this work, the near-surface elemental composition of a laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) processed Al-Mg-Si-Zr alloy was characterized by glow discharge optical emission spectroscopy GDOES depth profiling. The measurements reveal pronounced Mg enrichment within the near-surface region extending to approximately 10 μm, consistent with the characteristic scale of surface roughness, together with an increase in oxygen concentration, whereas Al, Si, and Zr approach stable bulk-like levels at greater depths. To understand this observation on the atomic scale, first-principles calculations based on density functional theory (DFT) were performed on low-index Al surfaces. The calculated results show a strong thermodynamic driving force for Mg surface segregation, with diffusion energy differences ranging from approximately -0.30 eV to -0.41 eV, while Zr exhibits a pronounced preference for remaining in the bulk matrix. Vacancy migration calculations further demonstrate that full structural relaxation substantially reduces the migration barrier for Mg to below that of Si, which makes Mg diffusion kinetically highly favorable. Moreover, the presence of adsorbed surface oxygen dramatically promotes the tendency of Mg to diffuse toward the surface, which lowers the diffusion energy difference of Mg to as much as -3.0 eV. This promotes the formation of a locally reconstructed Mg-O-Al coordinated precursor structure accompanied by localized electron transfer shown by an electron localization function analysis.

AI.tldr: GDOES depth profiling and DFT calculations reveal pronounced Mg enrichment (~10 μm) near the surface of an additively manufactured Al-Mg-Si-Zr alloy, driven by a strong thermodynamic and kinetic preference for Mg surface segregation that is further enhanced by adsorbed oxygen.
AI.motivation: Surface chemistry of additively manufactured aluminum alloys critically affects corrosion resistance and joining with external materials, yet the atomic-scale origin of near-surface elemental redistribution in PBF-LB/M Al-Mg-Si-Zr alloys remains unclear.
AI.method: Glow discharge optical emission spectroscopy (GDOES) depth profiling of a laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) Al-Mg-Si-Zr alloy; first-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations on low-index Al surfaces, including surface segregation energetics, vacancy migration barriers, and electron localization function (ELF) analysis.
AI.result: GDOES shows pronounced Mg enrichment and increased oxygen in the near-surface region extending to ~10 μm (consistent with surface roughness scale), while Al, Si, and Zr reach bulk-like levels at greater depths. DFT gives Mg segregation energy differences of about -0.30 to -0.41 eV, whereas Zr prefers the bulk. Full structural relaxation lowers the Mg vacancy migration barrier below that of Si, making Mg diffusion kinetically favorable, and adsorbed surface oxygen lowers the Mg diffusion energy difference to as much as -3.0 eV, promoting a locally reconstructed Mg-O-Al coordinated precursor with localized electron transfer.
AI.conclusion: Near-surface Mg enrichment in PBF-LB/M Al-Mg-Si-Zr is thermodynamically and kinetically favored, and is strongly promoted by adsorbed oxygen through formation of an Mg-O-Al coordinated precursor, explaining the observed surface chemistry relevant to corrosion and joining behavior.

title: Theoretical--operational modelling of complex experiments: parameter robustness and degeneracy in muon--electron conversion
summary: Complex experiments infer theory parameters through a coupled chain of physical models and data reduction. We formulate the theoretical--operational model (TOM) as a typed factorization of this forward prediction and study how changes of preparation, phenomenon modelling, readout, backgrounds, and analysis project onto the local manifold generated by the physics parameters. For a smooth prediction and a locally identifiable weighted least-squares estimate, the resulting response map separates each model deformation into a parameter-equivalent component and a residual component that cannot be absorbed by a change of the fitted physics parameters. This gives local criteria for robustness, exact degeneracy, and partial degeneracy of parameter inference. The construction is applied to charged-lepton-flavour-violating muon--electron conversion in aluminium. A one-bin conversion-rate model exhibits an exact normalization degeneracy. In a two-template model of the elastic--inelastic spectrum, a common signal normalization is absorbed by the fitted conversion rate without changing an operator-sensitive nuclear-response ratio, whereas a relative elastic--inelastic efficiency change is exactly parameter-equivalent to a change of that ratio at first order. A numerical Run-I example based on published Mu2e spectra shows that a \(100\,\mathrm{keV}/c\) momentum-scale mismatch is only partially parameter-equivalent: its projection ratio onto the local tangent space generated by the elastic normalization \(R_0\) and the logarithmic inelastic-to-elastic response ratio \(ρ\) is \(η=0.331\), while most of the weighted spectral deformation remains as a residual shape. TOM thereby provides a local theoretical description of parameter robustness and degeneracy at the interface of particle/nuclear phenomenology and experimental realization.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates the theoretical–operational model (TOM), a typed factorization of the forward prediction chain in complex experiments, to study how model deformations (preparation, phenomenon modelling, readout, backgrounds, analysis) project onto the local manifold of physics parameters. It yields local criteria for robustness, exact degeneracy, and partial degeneracy, and is applied to charged-lepton-flavour-violating muon–electron conversion in aluminium.
AI.motivation: Complex experiments infer theory parameters through a coupled chain of physical models and data reduction. There is a need for a local theoretical framework that quantifies how changes in each stage of this chain affect parameter inference, distinguishing deformations that can be absorbed by refitting physics parameters from those that cannot.
AI.method: The theoretical–operational model (TOM) is formulated as a typed factorization of the forward prediction. For a smooth prediction and a locally identifiable weighted least-squares estimate, the resulting response map decomposes each model deformation into a parameter-equivalent component and a residual component that cannot be absorbed by a change of fitted physics parameters. This decomposition provides local criteria for robustness, exact degeneracy, and partial degeneracy. The construction is applied to charged-lepton-flavour-violating muon–electron conversion in aluminium, using a one-bin conversion-rate model and a two-template model of the elastic–inelastic spectrum.
AI.result: A one-bin conversion-rate model exhibits an exact normalization degeneracy. In the two-template elastic–inelastic model, a common signal normalization is absorbed by the fitted conversion rate without changing an operator-sensitive nuclear-response ratio, whereas a relative elastic–inelastic efficiency change is exactly parameter-equivalent to a change of that ratio at first order. A numerical Run-I example based on published Mu2e spectra shows that a $100\,\mathrm{keV}/c$ momentum-scale mismatch is only partially parameter-equivalent: its projection ratio onto the local tangent space generated by the elastic normalization $R_0$ and the logarithmic inelastic-to-elastic response ratio $\rho$ is $\eta=0.331$, with most of the weighted spectral deformation remaining as a residual shape.
AI.conclusion: TOM provides a local theoretical description of parameter robustness and degeneracy at the interface of particle/nuclear phenomenology and experimental realization, enabling systematic identification of which model deformations are absorbable by parameter refitting and which leave irreducible residuals.

title: Parity anomaly governs the thermal Hall response of chiral superconductivity in rhombohedral graphene above and below $T_c$
summary: Chiral superconductivity has recently been confirmed in rhombohedral tetra- and pentalayer graphene near the BCS--BEC crossover, but no theory tells the experimentalist what thermal Hall response to expect, or why any signal should persist above the phase-coherence temperature $T_c$. We show that the parity anomaly of $(2{+}1)$-dimensional field theory fixes the answer exactly, at all temperatures, with no free parameters: $κ_{xy}/T = (π^2 k_B^2/6h)\,C_{\rm BdG}\,\tanh[Δ(T)/(2k_BT)]$, where $C_{\rm BdG}$ is the BdG Chern number and $Δ(T)$ is the fermionic excitation gap. The BCS--BEC two-gap relation $Δ^2 = Δ_{\rm sc}^2 + Δ_{\rm pg}^2$ makes the same formula govern both the condensate and pseudogap regimes, so the signal onsets at the pair-formation temperature $T^{*}$ rather than at $T_c$. Coleman--Hill non-renormalization and the $c_1 = 0$ theorem protect this result against interactions and finite-size artefacts. Three independent numerical validations confirm the topological input at machine precision (FHS Chern numbers, Wilson-loop $c_1 = 0$ test) and at the many-body level (DMRG on 28 converged ground states, including the real-space $p+ip$ signature $\arg\mathcal{A}_y - \arg\mathcal{A}_x = -π/2$ recovered to $10^{-14}$). The theory delivers an immediate falsifiable test that requires no new experimental apparatus: the sign of $κ_{xy}/T$ below $T_c$ must equal the sign of the anomalous Hall resistance $R_{xy}$ already measured above $T_c$, and four further predictions accessible by dilution-refrigerator nano-calorimetry on existing devices.

AI.tldr: The parity anomaly of (2+1)-dimensional field theory fixes the thermal Hall response of chiral superconductors in rhombohedral multilayer graphene exactly, with no free parameters, revealing that the signal onsets at the pair-formation temperature T* rather than Tc.
AI.motivation: Chiral superconductivity has recently been confirmed in rhombohedral tetra- and pentalayer graphene near the BCS-BEC crossover, but no existing theory tells experimentalists what thermal Hall response to expect, nor why any signal should persist above the phase-coherence temperature Tc. This lack of theoretical guidance motivates a parameter-free prediction that connects measurable thermal Hall signals to established experimental quantities.
AI.method: The authors derive the thermal Hall conductivity from the parity anomaly of (2+1)-dimensional field theory, obtaining κxy/T = (π²kB²/6h) C_BdG tanh[Δ(T)/(2kB T)], where C_BdG is the BdG Chern number and Δ(T) is the fermionic excitation gap. The BCS-BEC two-gap relation Δ² = Δsc² + Δpg² unifies condensate and pseudogap regimes. Coleman-Hill non-renormalization and the c1 = 0 theorem protect the result. Three independent numerical validations are performed: FHS Chern numbers, Wilson-loop c1 = 0 test, and DMRG on 28 converged ground states including the real-space p+ip signature arg Ay − arg Ax = −π/2.
AI.result: The formula governs both condensate and pseudogap regimes, so the thermal Hall signal onsets at the pair-formation temperature T* rather than at Tc. Numerical validations confirm the topological input to machine precision and at the many-body level (real-space p+ip signature recovered to 10⁻¹⁴). A falsifiable test is identified: the sign of κxy/T below Tc must equal the sign of the anomalous Hall resistance Rxy already measured above Tc, along with four further predictions accessible by dilution-refrigerator nano-calorimetry on existing devices.
AI.conclusion: The parity anomaly provides an exact, parameter-free thermal Hall response for chiral superconductors, linking the condensate and pseudogap regimes via the BCS-BEC two-gap relation. The result yields an immediate falsifiable test using existing experimental apparatus, requiring no new instrumentation, thereby bridging theory and accessible measurements in rhombohedral multilayer graphene.

title: Machine learning kinetics from molecular dynamics data
summary: Most molecular transitions occur on timescales far beyond direct molecular dynamics simulations. The committor, the probability that a configuration reaches a product state before a reactant state, is a central kinetic statistic, providing a mechanism-independent reaction coordinate and a foundation for transition path theory and the calculation of rates. This review surveys modern approaches for estimating the committor and related kinetic statistics from molecular simulations, with an emphasis on self-supervised methods that learn solutions of their defining dynamical equations rather than relying on labeled shooting data. We develop a common operator viewpoint connecting generator-based partial differential equations, variational principles, Markov state models, dynamical Galerkin approximation, and neural networks. Empirical and theoretical evidence points to the efficiency of these methods. We provide theoretical and practical guidance for realizing their full potential in applications, including strategies for treating non-Markovian effects and for sampling. We conclude by identifying opportunities for further research, including connections to reinforcement learning and generative modeling.

AI.tldr: A review of modern methods for estimating the committor and related kinetic statistics from molecular simulations, emphasizing self-supervised approaches that solve their defining dynamical equations rather than relying on labeled shooting data, unified through a common operator viewpoint.
AI.motivation: Most molecular transitions occur on timescales far beyond direct molecular dynamics simulations, making them difficult to study directly. The committor is a central kinetic statistic that provides a mechanism-independent reaction coordinate and underlies transition path theory and rate calculations, motivating the need for efficient estimation methods.
AI.method: The review surveys approaches for estimating the committor and related kinetic statistics. It develops a common operator viewpoint connecting generator-based partial differential equations, variational principles, Markov state models, dynamical Galerkin approximation, and neural networks, with emphasis on self-supervised methods that learn solutions of their defining dynamical equations.
AI.result: Empirical and theoretical evidence points to the efficiency of these self-supervised methods. The review also provides theoretical and practical guidance for realizing their full potential in applications, including strategies for treating non-Markovian effects and for sampling.
AI.conclusion: The review identifies opportunities for further research, including connections to reinforcement learning and generative modeling.

title: Structure of Measurement-Induced Entanglement in Infinite-Randomness Critical States
summary: The impact of projective measurements on a many-body quantum state is tightly linked to its underlying entanglement structure. Critical states are particularly sensitive, as long-range entanglement allows local measurements to have global consequences. This has been extensively studied in the context of critical states described by a conformal field theory (CFT), where measurements can alter critical properties in post-measurement quantities ('measurement-altered criticality') and induce long-range entanglement with universal features ('measurement-induced entanglement'). By contrast, little is known about the role of measurements on critical states with quenched disorder, which admit no CFT description. Here, we develop a theory of measurements on one-dimensional critical states governed by infinite-randomness fixed points (IRFPs), focusing on two closely related examples: the random XXZ chain and the random transverse-field Ising model. We show that the measurement-induced entanglement decays as a power-law with universal exponent $(3-\sqrt{5})/2$ in both models, and that the minimum number of measurements required to establish this entanglement obeys a universal scaling form. When only a finite density of measurements is made, we show that the critical properties of the state are remarkably robust: `measurement-altered criticality' is absent, with measurements either preserving the critical exponents, or destroying the criticality entirely. These results establish IRFPs as an analytically tractable arena for measurements on critical states, complementary to the CFT case. The outcome randomness that necessitates replica methods in clean systems becomes trivial at infinite randomness, with the universal response governed by the statistics induced by the quenched disorder.

AI.tldr: This work develops a theory of projective measurements on 1D critical states governed by infinite-randomness fixed points (IRFPs), using the random XXZ chain and random transverse-field Ising model. It finds universal measurement-induced entanglement decaying as a power law with exponent (3−√5)/2, a universal scaling form for the minimum number of measurements, and shows that with finite measurement density, either critical exponents are preserved or criticality is destroyed, with no measurement-altered criticality.
AI.motivation: Measurement effects on many-body critical states are well studied for conformal field theory (CFT) states, where local measurements cause global consequences and can yield measurement-altered criticality and measurement-induced entanglement. However, critical states with quenched disorder admit no CFT description, and the role of measurements on such states—specifically those governed by infinite-randomness fixed points—remains largely unknown. This paper addresses that gap.
AI.method: The authors develop an analytic theory of projective measurements on one-dimensional critical states governed by infinite-randomness fixed points, focusing on the random XXZ chain and the random transverse-field Ising model. They leverage the trivialization of outcome randomness at infinite randomness, which renders replica methods unnecessary, and analyze the statistics induced by quenched disorder to extract universal behavior.
AI.result: Measurement-induced entanglement decays as a power law with a universal exponent (3−√5)/2 in both models. The minimum number of measurements needed to establish this entanglement follows a universal scaling form. Under a finite density of measurements, the critical properties are robust: measurement-altered criticality is absent, and measurements either preserve the critical exponents or destroy criticality entirely.
AI.conclusion: IRFPs provide an analytically tractable setting for studying measurements on critical states, complementing the CFT framework. The outcome randomness that normally requires replica methods in clean systems becomes trivial at infinite randomness, and the universal response is governed by quenched-disorder-induced statistics.

title: Entropy spectroscopy of a tunable two-site Hubbard molecule
comment: 21 pages, 5 figures, Supplementary Materials 16 pages, 7 figures
summary: Determining which microscopic states remain thermally active when tunneling and interactions compete is a central question in Hubbard physics. Here we develop an entropy measurement protocol for a double quantum dot, extending the charge-based approach established for a single dot, and measure the total entropy of a tunable two-site Hubbard molecule realized in a GaAs double dot. By shifting both dot levels together at fixed detuning, the entropy is correctly probed with only a single charge sensor. As interdot tunneling increases, the system evolves from two atomic-like dots through hybridized molecular states to a merged single dot. Across this evolution, the entropy decreases as tunnel-induced energy splitting exceeds the thermal energy and suppresses the occupation of higher-energy states. The measurements resolve the diminishing contribution of antibonding states and the changing thermal contributions of hybridized singlet and triplet states, in quantitative agreement with a two-site Hubbard model. By distinguishing states with the same charge configuration but different orbital and spin content, entropy reveals how tunneling and interactions determine the thermally active states of the minimal Hubbard system.

AI.tldr: The authors develop an entropy measurement protocol for a GaAs double quantum dot and measure the total entropy of a tunable two-site Hubbard molecule, tracking the evolution from atomic-like dots through hybridized molecular states to a merged single dot.
AI.motivation: Determining which microscopic states remain thermally active when tunneling and interactions compete is a central question in Hubbard physics, motivating a direct thermodynamic probe of the minimal two-site Hubbard system.
AI.method: They extend the charge-based entropy measurement approach established for a single dot to a double quantum dot. By shifting both dot levels together at fixed detuning, entropy is probed with only a single charge sensor.
AI.result: As interdot tunneling increases, the system evolves from two atomic-like dots through hybridized molecular states to a merged single dot, with entropy decreasing as tunnel-induced splitting exceeds thermal energy. The measurements resolve the diminishing contribution of antibonding states and the changing thermal contributions of hybridized singlet and triplet states, in quantitative agreement with a two-site Hubbard model.
AI.conclusion: By distinguishing states with the same charge configuration but different orbital and spin content, entropy reveals how tunneling and interactions determine the thermally active states of the minimal Hubbard system.

title: Electrostatic quadrupole lens for focusing a cryogenic $^{205}$TlF molecular beam
summary: Precision measurements with molecules require molecular beams with high flux and narrow divergence. Here we present the design, implementation, and characterization of an electrostatic quadrupole lens (EQL) for focusing a cryogenic beam of $^{205}$TlF molecules. The EQL consists of four electrodes operated at spatially alternating potentials up to $\pm 30$ kV. This configuration generates a transverse restoring force that focuses molecules prepared in selected manifold of hyperfine states. At the optimal applied voltage, the EQL increases the detected molecular signal by a factor of $14.4(4)$ at the current detection position. The measured lens gain, transverse Doppler spectra, and transverse spatial profiles are all reproduced by trajectory simulations using independently measured beam parameters as input. Based on this agreement, we project a gain of $16.5(8)$ for the full $7.9~\mathrm{m}$ CeNTREX beamline. These results establish the EQL as a key component for increasing sensitivity in precision experiments using cryogenic beams of polar molecules.

AI.tldr: An electrostatic quadrupole lens focuses a cryogenic TlF molecular beam, boosting detected signal by 14.4x and projecting 16.5x gain over the full beamline, validated by trajectory simulations.
AI.motivation: Precision measurements with molecules demand molecular beams that simultaneously have high flux and narrow divergence. Improving these beam properties is essential for increasing the sensitivity of precision experiments using cryogenic beams of polar molecules.
AI.method: The authors designed, implemented, and characterized an electrostatic quadrupole lens (EQL) for focusing a cryogenic beam of 205TlF molecules. The EQL uses four electrodes with spatially alternating potentials up to ±30 kV, producing a transverse restoring force that focuses molecules in a selected manifold of hyperfine states. They compared measurements (lens gain, transverse Doppler spectra, transverse spatial profiles) against trajectory simulations using independently measured beam parameters.
AI.result: At optimal applied voltage, the EQL increases the detected molecular signal by a factor of 14.4(4) at the current detection position. The measured lens gain, transverse Doppler spectra, and transverse spatial profiles are all reproduced by trajectory simulations. Based on this agreement, the authors project a gain of 16.5(8) for the full 7.9 m CeNTREX beamline.
AI.conclusion: The EQL is established as a key component for increasing sensitivity in precision experiments using cryogenic beams of polar molecules.

title: Spectroscopy of deprotonated anions of cold chlorophyll pigments, an approach to their photosynthetic properties
summary: We introduce here a new approach to the study of isolated chlorophyll pigments with the electronic spectroscopy of their deprotonated anions in a cold environment at 9K. These anions are isoelectronic to the corresponding neutral molecules, therefore their electronic properties are comparable. This comparison is pursued through this article. The electronic spectrum of the Q bands of deprotonated pheophorbide and methyl pheophorbide are recorded by resonant two photon electron detachment with vibrational resolution and show well-resolved bands extending through the visible spectrum in a very similar fashion to their neutral counterparts in solution. The results are compared with data of neutral pheophytin obtained by fluorescence line narrowing spectroscopy at 4K and resonance Raman spectroscopy and found very similar. The theoretical analysis is achieved by density functional (ground state DFT WB97XD, hybrid exchange-correlation functionals and 6-311++G(d,p) basis sets) and time dependent density functional (TDDFT) calculations. The comparison of the active orbitals in the Q transitions shows a great similarity between neutral and anionic forms together with some orbital and related level inversions. The vibronic spectra are simulated by Franck-Condon calculations to assign the dominant transitions of the electronic spectrum. Globally, this is a new perspective in the electronic spectroscopy of chlorophyll pigments that has been opened.

AI.tldr: Electronic spectroscopy of deprotonated chlorophyll anions at 9K reveals Q-band spectra closely resembling their neutral counterparts, validated by DFT/TDDFT and Franck-Condon simulations, offering a new perspective on chlorophyll pigment spectroscopy.
AI.motivation: Studying isolated chlorophyll pigments is challenging, so the authors exploit deprotonated anions that are isoelectronic to the neutral molecules, allowing their electronic properties to be compared directly with neutral counterparts.
AI.method: Q-band electronic spectra of deprotonated pheophorbide and methyl pheophorbide were recorded by resonant two-photon electron detachment with vibrational resolution at 9K. Results were compared with fluorescence line narrowing (4K) and resonance Raman data of neutral pheophytin. Theoretical analysis used DFT (WB97XD, hybrid functionals, 6-311++G(d,p)) and TDDFT, with Franck-Condon simulations for vibronic spectra.
AI.result: Well-resolved Q-band spectra extending across the visible region were obtained, very similar to neutral counterparts in solution. Active orbitals in the Q transitions show strong similarity between neutral and anionic forms, with some orbital and level inversions. Franck-Condon simulations assigned the dominant electronic transitions.
AI.conclusion: Comparing deprotonated anions to neutral chlorophylls provides a new perspective in the electronic spectroscopy of chlorophyll pigments.

title: Enabling Polaritonic Electronic Structure Theory for Psi4: The psi4-cbo package
summary: We present psi4-cbo, an open-source extension of the Psi4 program for simulations within the cavity Born-Oppenheimer Approximation (CBOA). By treating the cavity photon mode on the same footing as the nuclear coordinates, \texttt{psi4-cbo} incorporates light-matter coupling into standard electronic structure workflows. These workflows include self-consistent field calculations, response theory, analytic gradients, joint Hessians, and geometry optimization. The package is designed for reproducibility and is documented with working examples for its main workflows. To evaluate the approximations inherent to the CBOA framework, we use an exact \gls{qedfci} reference. Resolving the correlation energy into electron-electron and electron-photon channels enables us to precisely determine the point at which the CBOA becomes quantitatively sufficient. Additionally, we highlight that, since self-consistent treatments dress the cavity modes, satisfying experimental resonance conditions is method-dependent. As a practical application, we investigate the chromophore acrolein under vibrational strong coupling and detail how to locate resonances on the dressed photon modes rather than the bare molecular bands.

AI.tldr: psi4-cbo extends Psi4 to simulate cavity Born-Oppenheimer Approximation (CBOA) workflows, integrating cavity photon modes into standard electronic structure methods, and benchmarks CBOA accuracy against exact QED-FCI while showing how self-consistent dressing shifts resonance conditions.
AI.motivation: To provide an open-source, reproducible tool for light-matter coupling within standard electronic structure workflows, and to determine quantitatively when the CBOA is sufficient by comparing against an exact QED-FCI reference, while clarifying how cavity dressing affects experimental resonance conditions.
AI.method: psi4-cbo treats the cavity photon mode on equal footing with nuclear coordinates, enabling self-consistent field, response theory, analytic gradients, joint Hessians, and geometry optimization. CBOA approximations are evaluated against exact QED-FCI, with the correlation energy decomposed into electron-electron and electron-photon channels, and acrolein under vibrational strong coupling is studied by locating resonances on dressed photon modes.
AI.result: The point at which CBOA becomes quantitatively sufficient is precisely identified via the electron-electron/electron-photon correlation energy decomposition. Self-consistent treatments dress the cavity modes, making satisfaction of experimental resonance conditions method-dependent; resonances for acrolein under vibrational strong coupling are located on dressed photon modes rather than bare molecular bands.
AI.conclusion: psi4-cbo offers a documented, reproducible open-source platform for CBOA-based simulations and provides quantitative guidance on CBOA validity. Because self-consistent dressing makes resonance conditions method-dependent, resonances should be located on dressed photon modes, as demonstrated for acrolein under vibrational strong coupling.

title: What does "instant thermalization" in large-$q$ SYK models mean?
summary:
Motivated by the Planckian thermalization rate $Γ\sim T$ observed in the two-body interacting SYK model, we study thermalization in the $q/2$-body case. Previous studies of such systems have established the notion of instantaneous thermalization to leading order in $1/q$. It was conjectured that the thermalization may still be Planckian but with a divergent rate $Γ\sim T q$, explaining the ``instantaneous'' part. For an analytically and numerically tractable system, we calculate the effective temperatures after a quench at time $t = 0$ and indeed find a Planckian rate, albeit with the unexpected decaying behavior $Γ\sim T q^{-1} $. This is contrasted with the behavior of the causal Green's function $\mathcal{G}(t_1, t_2)$, which instantly acquires a thermal form in the two-time plane block $t_1, t_2 > 0$.
  The resulting picture is that instant thermalization is a meaningful concept only for this block, while the off-diagonal blocks $t_1 \cdot t_2 < 0$ are inherently non-thermal at any $q$. Since the effective temperature is obtained from correlations spanning all blocks, it inherits a finite rate set by the off-diagonal. We illustrate this directly by studying the non-thermal correlations' time dependence.

AI.tldr: The paper studies thermalization in the $q/2$-body interacting SYK model. Contrary to the conjectured Planckian rate $\\Gamma \\sim T q$, the authors find a Planckian but decaying rate $\\Gamma \\sim T q^{-1}$. They show that instant thermalization holds only for the $t_1, t_2 > 0$ block of the causal Green's function, while off-diagonal blocks ($t_1 t_2 < 0$) remain non-thermal at any $q$, and this non-thermality sets the finite effective thermalization rate.
AI.motivation: Motivated by the Planckian thermalization rate $\\Gamma \\sim T$ observed in the two-body interacting SYK model, the authors investigate whether thermalization in the $q/2$-body case remains Planckian. Prior work established instantaneous thermalization to leading order in $1/q$ and conjectured a divergent Planckian rate $\\Gamma \\sim T q$ to explain this instantaneous behavior, which they aim to test in a tractable system.
AI.method: The authors use an analytically and numerically tractable system. They calculate the effective temperatures after a quench at $t = 0$, extracting the thermalization rate. They also analyze the behavior of the causal Green's function $\\mathcal{G}(t_1, t_2)$ in different regions of the two-time plane, specifically the diagonal block ($t_1, t_2 > 0$) and off-diagonal blocks ($t_1 t_2 < 0$), and study the time dependence of the non-thermal correlations directly.
AI.result: They find a Planckian rate, but with the unexpected decaying behavior $\\Gamma \\sim T q^{-1}$ rather than the conjectured divergent $\\Gamma \\sim T q$. The causal Green's function instantly acquires a thermal form in the diagonal block $t_1, t_2 > 0$, while the off-diagonal blocks $t_1 t_2 < 0$ are inherently non-thermal at any $q$.
AI.conclusion: Instant thermalization is a meaningful concept only for the diagonal block ($t_1, t_2 > 0$) of the causal Green's function. Since the effective temperature is obtained from correlations spanning all blocks, it inherits a finite rate set by the off-diagonal non-thermal blocks, which is responsible for the $\\Gamma \\sim T q^{-1}$ scaling. The off-diagonal blocks remain non-thermal at any $q$, and this is illustrated by studying the non-thermal correlations' time dependence.

title: A Scaling Framework for Mechanical Memristance: Dimensionless Metrics and Material Design Maps
summary: Mechanical memristors are systems whose dissipative response depends on the history of previous loading through an evolving internal state. History-dependent forces and dissipation occur in a wide range of materials and devices, including viscoelastic polymers, shape-memory materials, piezoelectrics, granular media and field-responsive fluids. Determining which of these responses admits a mechanical-memristor representation requires a constitutive test, as well as a comparison of scales. In this work, a fractional-order mechanical memristor model is developed and cast into a nondimensional form to identify the governing parameters controlling memory-dependent dissipation. The formulation leads to a set of dimensionless groups that characterise dissipation magnitude, memory-state scale and memory transfer. These quantities are combined into an effective mechanical memristance screening index \(\Mh = βγ|\mathcal H_α(Ω)|\), which provides a conditional measure of local damping modulation at matched response amplitude, constitutive slope and reference scales. Illustrative parameter scenarios are then constructed for material classes including shape-memory polymers, shape-memory alloys, hydrogels, nanocellulose, lignin-rich materials, natural fibres, piezoelectric polymers, piezoelectric ceramics, electrorheological fluids, magnetorheological fluids and granular dampers. The framework establishes a common basis for comparing memory-dependent damping within the adopted constitutive description and identifies the calibration required for its application to candidate materials and devices

AI.tldr: A fractional-order mechanical memristor model is developed in nondimensional form, yielding a screening index for memory-dependent damping that is compared across many material classes.
AI.motivation: History-dependent forces and dissipation appear in many materials (viscoelastic polymers, shape-memory materials, piezoelectrics, granular media, field-responsive fluids), but it is unclear which responses genuinely admit a mechanical-memristor representation. A constitutive test and scale comparison are needed.
AI.method: A fractional-order mechanical memristor model is formulated and cast into nondimensional form, exposing the governing parameters of memory-dependent dissipation. This yields dimensionless groups for dissipation magnitude, memory-state scale, and memory transfer, combined into an effective mechanical memristance screening index Mh = beta*gamma*|H_alpha(Omega)|. Illustrative parameter scenarios are constructed for multiple material classes.
AI.result: The screening index provides a conditional measure of local damping modulation at matched response amplitude, constitutive slope, and reference scales. Parameter scenarios are generated for shape-memory polymers and alloys, hydrogels, nanocellulose, lignin-rich materials, natural fibres, piezoelectric polymers and ceramics, electrorheological and magnetorheological fluids, and granular dampers.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a common basis for comparing memory-dependent damping within the adopted constitutive description and identifies the calibration needed to apply it to candidate materials and devices.

title: Magnetically coupled charge-transport crossover and giant negative magnetoresistance in iodine-incorporated Cr$_2$Se$_3$
summary: We report the synthesis and comprehensive investigation of iodine-incorporated $Cr_2Se_3$, a non-van der Waals quasi-two-dimensional magnetic material, using structural, magnetic, transport, spectroscopic, and first-principles methods. Magnetization and electron spin resonance measurements reveal an antiferromagnetically ordered state below $T_N \approx 52$ K. At higher temperatures, a second, broader anomaly emerges near $T^* \approx 150$ K, coinciding with a shallow minimum in the temperature-dependent resistivity that resembles a metal-to-insulator-like crossover. Hall measurements indicate predominantly hole-like conduction at high temperatures ($\geq$ 150 K), while the nonlinear Hall response below T*, together with an anomaly in the third-harmonic electrical signal, suggests the emergence of mobility-dependent multichannel and spatially inhomogeneous transport. A large, non-saturating negative magnetoresistance reaching approximately -78\% at 25 K and 12 T further demonstrates strong coupling between charge transport and the magnetic state. Temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy reveals no symmetry-changing structural transition near T*, whereas angle resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) measurements show no major reconstruction of the electronic structure occupied across the crossover. Taken together, these results identify the high-temperature anomaly as a broad magnetically coupled transport crossover arising from the interplay of short-range magnetic correlations, chemical disorder, and redistribution among competing conduction channels. These findings demonstrate that anion incorporation provides an effective route to tuning the coupled electronic and magnetic properties of non-layered Cr$_2$Se$_3$, establishing this system as a promising platform for investigating correlated transport and emergent spintronic functionalities in transition-metal chalcogenides.

AI.tldr: Iodine-incorporated Cr2Se3, a non-van der Waals quasi-2D magnet, shows AFM order at TN ~ 52 K and a broader magnetically coupled transport crossover near T* ~ 150 K driven by short-range magnetic correlations, chemical disorder, and competing conduction channels.
AI.motivation: Non-layered (non-van der Waals) transition-metal chalcogenides such as Cr2Se3 are less explored than layered counterparts, yet offer tunability via anion incorporation. The authors aim to determine how anionic (iodine) substitution modifies the coupled electronic and magnetic properties and to clarify the origin of a high-temperature transport anomaly.
AI.method: Synthesis of iodine-incorporated Cr2Se3, characterized by magnetization, electron spin resonance, resistivity, Hall and third-harmonic transport measurements, temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy, ARPES, and first-principles calculations.
AI.result: Antiferromagnetic order below TN ~ 52 K; a second broad anomaly near T* ~ 150 K coinciding with a shallow resistivity minimum (metal-to-insulator-like crossover); hole-like conduction above 150 K, nonlinear Hall response and third-harmonic anomaly below T* indicating multichannel, spatially inhomogeneous transport; large non-saturating negative magnetoresistance of ~-78% at 25 K and 12 T; Raman shows no symmetry-changing structural transition and ARPES shows no major occupied-band reconstruction across the crossover.
AI.conclusion: The high-temperature anomaly is a broad magnetically coupled transport crossover arising from short-range magnetic correlations, chemical disorder, and redistribution among competing conduction channels. Anion incorporation is an effective route to tune coupled electronic and magnetic properties of non-layered Cr2Se3, positioning it as a platform for correlated transport and emergent spintronic functionality in transition-metal chalcogenides.

title: Nitrogen based electride superconductor Nb5Ir3N under pressure: multifunctional physical properties from DFT based first-principles investigation
summary: Discovery and study of superconducting electrides have opened new avenues in condensed matter physics, driven by their intriguing multifunctional features spanning ambient and high-pressure regimes. This work investigates the ternary nitride superconductor Nb5Ir3N under pressure ranging from 0 to 20 GPa via density functional theory based simulations. Estimated structural parameters agree well with the available data, confirming their reliability and supporting the validity of this analysis. Negative formation enthalpy, together with evaluated elastic constants and phonon spectra, confirm the structural, thermodynamic, mechanical, and dynamical stability of Nb5Ir3N over the entire pressure range. Pressure dependent elastic constants and polycrystalline elastic moduli are investigated. The compound is categorized as ductile in light of estimated mechanical indices. Elastic anisotropy factors indicate that Nb5Ir3N remains anisotropic, with the degree of anisotropy gradually decreasing as pressure increases. Electronic band structure and density of states are calculated with and without spin orbit coupling to investigate its influence on the electronic structure. Calculated optical response reveals substantial intraband contributions in the low energy region, intense ultraviolet absorption, and strong reflectivity. The spectra exhibit optical anisotropy and a broadening at higher pressures. Pressure induced superconducting features are also discussed qualitatively.

AI.tldr: This DFT study examines the ternary nitride superconductor Nb5Ir3N under 0–20 GPa, confirming its stability, ductility, elastic anisotropy, electronic and optical properties including spin-orbit coupling effects, and discussing pressure-induced superconductivity qualitatively.
AI.motivation: Superconducting electrides, including ternary nitride superconductors, are of broad interest in condensed matter physics due to their multifunctional properties spanning ambient and high-pressure regimes. Understanding how pressure tunes the structural, mechanical, electronic, optical, and superconducting behavior of such materials motivates this investigation of Nb5Ir3N.
AI.method: Density functional theory (DFT) based simulations were performed on Nb5Ir3N over a pressure range of 0 to 20 GPa. Structural parameters, formation enthalpy, elastic constants, polycrystalline elastic moduli, mechanical indices, elastic anisotropy factors, and phonon spectra were computed. Electronic band structure and density of states were calculated with and without spin-orbit coupling, and optical response spectra were evaluated.
AI.result: Estimated structural parameters agree well with available data. Negative formation enthalpy, elastic constants, and phonon spectra confirm structural, thermodynamic, mechanical, and dynamical stability across the entire pressure range. Nb5Ir3N is ductile and remains anisotropic, with anisotropy gradually decreasing under pressure. Optical response shows substantial intraband contributions at low energy, intense ultraviolet absorption, strong reflectivity, optical anisotropy, and broadening at higher pressures. Pressure-induced superconducting features are discussed qualitatively.
AI.conclusion: Nb5Ir3N is a structurally, mechanically, and dynamically stable ductile superconductor whose anisotropy and optical properties are tunable with pressure, and whose superconducting behavior is qualitatively pressure-dependent, highlighting it as a promising multifunctional material for high-pressure applications.

title: MLegS: A modern mapped Legendre spectral method solver for unbounded domains with parallelization
summary: MLegS is an open-source Modern Fortran code package for solving linear and nonlinear time-dependent partial differential equations on radially unbounded domains. It builds on an earlier in-house prototype, recasting it as a modular solver with a unified interface for fields, transforms, and spectral operators. Within this framework, the numerical formulation maps $0\leq r<\infty$ onto a finite interval, where associated Legendre functions provide the radial basis, while Fourier series represent the periodic azimuthal and axial directions. The mapped radial basis represents radial infinity without imposing an artificial boundary condition at finite radius while incorporating the regularity required at $r=0$ according to azimuthal order. The implementation distributes the corresponding field layouts using the Message-Passing Interface (MPI), with strong- and weak-scaling measurements extending to 512 cores across four compute nodes. Beyond parallel performance, three examples assess the solver across diffusion, reaction-diffusion, and vortex dynamics: closed-form diffusion solutions establish spectral spatial convergence and the design orders of both semi-implicit integrators; a Fisher-Kolmogorov-Petrovsky-Piskunov front matches the linearized solution and propagates at the classical speed within its logarithmic correction; and vortex-pair simulations based on toroidal-poloidal decomposition yield a measured Crow growth rate $2.7\%$ above the theoretical prediction and demonstrate the reconnection of the vortex pair.

AI.tldr: MLegS is a modular open-source modern Fortran spectral solver for linear and nonlinear time-dependent PDEs on radially unbounded domains, using mapped associated Legendre functions radially and Fourier series azimuthally/axially, MPI-parallelized up to 512 cores, validated on diffusion, reaction-diffusion, and vortex dynamics benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Time-dependent PDEs on radially unbounded domains are difficult to solve because radial infinity must be represented without artificial far-field boundary conditions, while also enforcing the regularity condition at the origin that depends on azimuthal order. The work promotes an earlier in-house prototype into a reusable, modular, and parallel code package.
AI.method: The code maps $0\leq r<\infty$ onto a finite interval and uses associated Legendre functions as the radial basis, embedding the $r=0$ regularity condition according to azimuthal order and representing radial infinity without an artificial finite-radius boundary condition. Fourier series handle the periodic azimuthal and axial directions. The package provides a unified interface for fields, transforms, and spectral operators, with radial-parallel field layouts distributed via MPI. Temporal integration uses two semi-implicit integrators of prescribed design order.
AI.result: Strong- and weak-scaling measurements extend to 512 cores across four compute nodes. Closed-form diffusion solutions establish spectral spatial convergence and the design orders of both semi-implicit integrators. A Fisher-Kolmogorov-Petrovsky-Piskunov front matches the linearized solution and propagates at the classical speed within its logarithmic correction. Vortex-pair simulations using toroidal-poloidal decomposition yield a measured Crow growth rate $2.7\%$ above the theoretical prediction and demonstrate vortex-pair reconnection.
AI.conclusion: MLegS provides a compact, modular, and MPI-parallel spectral framework for linear and nonlinear time-dependent PDEs on radially unbounded domains, with verified convergence, integrator order, and physical fidelity across diffusion, reaction-diffusion, and vortex dynamics problems.

title: Macroscopic Response Diagnoses the Noise Sensitivity of Terminal Outcomes
summary: Can the terminal macroscopic outcome of a many-body system be inferred from its microscopic initial data without simulating the full trajectory? Rather than construct such a shortcut, we address a more fundamental question for Gaussian microscopic inputs: can any fixed Wiener-Hermite degree retain a nonvanishing fraction of the variance of the terminal outcome as the system grows? We consider homogeneous systems with independent Gaussian disorder in which all microscopic coordinates are symmetry-equivalent, the terminal event is monotone in each disorder variable, and a uniform disorder shift is exactly equivalent to a control-field shift with a size-independent conversion factor. Using forward and inverse Gaussian influence bounds together with a Gaussian Russo formula, we derive a directly measurable criterion that is both necessary and sufficient for noise sensitivity. Specifically, the correlation between the original and coordinate-perturbed terminal outcomes vanishes asymptotically for every fixed nonzero level of coordinatewise noise if and only if the slope of the outcome probability with respect to the control field at the balanced threshold grows more slowly than the square root of the system volume. Event-driven simulations of the three-dimensional driven random-field Ising model up to linear size 192 find that both the normalized response and the correlations between perturbed samples decrease overall, consistent with the noise-sensitive regime at finite size. For spatial Stag-Hunt dynamics with prescribed seeds, the criterion generalizes through an effective number of influential coordinates. Separately, simulations of a path-dependent best-response game show, over the sizes studied, that the terminal equilibrium can depend on the update schedule while still carrying substantial finite-order predictive information.

AI.tldr: The paper asks whether any fixed Wiener-Hermite (fixed-order noise) representation can retain a nonvanishing share of the variance of a many-body system's terminal macroscopic outcome as the system grows, and derives a necessary-and-sufficient measurable criterion for asymptotic noise sensitivity for Gaussian microscopic inputs.
AI.motivation: Predicting the terminal macroscopic outcome of a many-body system from initial data usually requires simulating the full trajectory, which is intractable. A shortcut is hard to construct, so the authors instead probe a more fundamental question: for Gaussian microscopic inputs, can any fixed Wiener-Hermite degree preserve a nonvanishing fraction of the terminal-outcome variance as system size grows?
AI.method: They study homogeneous systems with independent Gaussian disorder, symmetry-equivalent microscopic coordinates, terminal events monotone in each disorder variable, and a uniform disorder shift exactly equivalent to a control-field shift with size-independent conversion factor. They combine forward and inverse Gaussian influence bounds with a Gaussian Russo formula to derive a directly measurable noise-sensitivity criterion, and test it via event-driven simulations of the three-dimensional driven random-field Ising model up to linear size 192. They also generalize to spatial Stag-Hunt dynamics via an effective number of influential coordinates, and simulate a path-dependent best-response game.
AI.result: The correlation between original and coordinate-perturbed terminal outcomes vanishes asymptotically for every fixed nonzero level of coordinatewise noise if and only if the slope of the outcome probability with respect to the control field at the balanced threshold grows more slowly than the square root of the system volume. Simulations up to linear size 192 show both normalized response and inter-perturbed-sample correlations decrease overall, consistent with the noise-sensitive regime at finite size. The Stag-Hunt criterion generalizes through an effective number of influential coordinates, and the path-dependent best-response game's terminal equilibrium can depend on the update schedule while retaining substantial finite-order predictive information.
AI.conclusion: Fixed Wiener-Hermite degree cannot generally retain a nonvanishing variance fraction as the system grows; noise sensitivity admits a sharp, measurable necessary-and-sufficient criterion based on the scaling of the threshold control-field slope versus the square root of system volume, supported by finite-size simulations and extended to additional dynamics.

title: A semiconductor photon-pair source based on a polariton cascade
summary: We present a theoretical study of a semiconductor photon-pair source based on a radiative cascade enabled by a permanent exciton dipole. The source consists of a GaAs quantum dot placed between a metal nanoparticle and a mirror. The dot exciton and the localized electromagnetic mode mix to form upper and lower polaritons. Without a permanent dipole, a symmetry separating states with even and odd excitation numbers forbids photon emission between the polaritons. Separation of the mean electron and hole positions gives the exciton a permanent dipole and breaks this symmetry. The upper polariton can then emit an idler photon as it decays to the lower polariton. The lower polariton can emit a signal photon as the system returns to its ground state. Using an effective model, we calculate the probability that a prepared upper polariton emits both photons through the metal antenna. We also analyse fluctuations in the emitted photon counts and correlations between the two emission channels. The calculation establishes an operating principle for assumed emitter properties and optical loss rates. Whether the device can be built and its photon correlations measured remains open.

AI.tldr: Theoretical study of a photon-pair source using a GaAs quantum dot coupled to a metal nanoparticle-mirror cavity, where a permanent exciton dipole breaks the even/odd excitation symmetry and enables polariton-mediated cascade emission of idler and signal photons.
AI.motivation: Conventional radiative-cascade photon-pair sources rely on level structure that forbids photon emission between polariton states due to a symmetry separating even and odd excitation numbers. A mechanism is needed to break this symmetry so that cascaded two-photon emission through a polariton channel becomes allowed.
AI.method: The system is a GaAs quantum dot placed between a metal nanoparticle and a mirror. The dot exciton hybridizes with the localized electromagnetic mode to form upper and lower polaritons. Separation of mean electron and hole positions gives the exciton a permanent dipole, breaking the parity symmetry. An effective model is used to calculate the probability that a prepared upper polariton emits both photons through the metal antenna, together with fluctuations in emitted photon counts and correlations between the two emission channels.
AI.result: With the permanent dipole present, the upper polariton can emit an idler photon while decaying to the lower polariton, and the lower polariton can emit a signal photon as the system returns to its ground state. The calculation yields the two-photon emission probability and the photon-count statistics and channel correlations, establishing an operating principle for assumed emitter properties and optical loss rates.
AI.conclusion: The work proposes an operating principle for a permanent-dipole-enabled polariton cascade photon-pair source, but whether the device can be realized and its photon correlations measured remains an open question.

title: Second-Order Rayleigh-Schrödinger Perturbation Theory for the GRASP2018 Package: Three-Particle Feynman Diagram Contribution to Valence-Valence Correlations
summary: The method based on the second-order perturbation theory to identify the most important configuration state functions of the various correlations is extended to include valence-valence correlations, which are described by the three-particle Feynman diagram. The extension presented in this work complements the core-valence, core, core-core, and valence-valence correlations which were developed in a series of previous papers by G. Gaigalas, P. Rynkun and L. Kitovienė. Whereas these valence-valence correlations are described by the three-particle Feynman diagram, additional developments to calculate the spin-angular parts of this diagram have been made to the program library librang of the Grasp. As an example of the application of the developed method, the atomic calculations of the energy structure for the Se III are presented. In the present work, this method was also used to select the most significant configuration state functions and to use this basis to solve the self-consistent field equations.

AI.tldr: The second-order perturbation theory method for identifying important configuration state functions is extended to valence-valence correlations via a three-particle Feynman diagram, implemented in the Grasp librang library, and applied to Se III energy structure calculations.
AI.motivation: Previous work by Gaigalas, Rynkun, and Kitovienė developed correlations (core-valence, core, core-core) but had not yet included valence-valence correlations, which are needed for a complete treatment of correlation effects in atomic structure calculations.
AI.method: The second-order perturbation theory method is extended to valence-valence correlations described by a three-particle Feynman diagram. Spin-angular parts of this diagram were calculated through additional developments to the librang program library of Grasp. This method selects the most significant configuration state functions, which are then used as a basis to solve the self-consistent field equations.
AI.result: Atomic calculations of the energy structure for Se III were performed as an application example, demonstrating the extended method's utility.
AI.conclusion: The extension complements prior correlation treatments and provides a practical approach for selecting important configuration state functions and solving self-consistent field equations, as demonstrated in Se III.

title: Hydrodynamic memory in overdamped colloidal dynamics
summary: Micron-sized colloid particles diffusing through a fluid experience hydrodynamic inertial and memory effects, the latter causing velocity autocorrelation to decay as a power law. At the same time, many theoretical descriptions treat colloidal diffusion in a fluid using overdamped Langevin dynamics for its convenience, eliminating velocity, omitting inertia, but also ignoring the power-law memory. In this Letter, we show that hydrodynamic memory survives in the overdamped (colloid-inertialess) limit. By identifying the dimensionless parameter controlling the crossover between early- and late-time dynamics, we derive in closed form the overdamped Langevin equation in the presence of hydrodynamic memory. This provides a theoretical framework for realistically describing colloidal dynamics in a fluid, and establishes a rigorous basis for the positional memory observed in high-resolution experiments. Our theory predicts that hydrodynamic memory becomes increasingly pronounced for smaller particles and under stronger external forcing, and offers experimental probes for the crossover from conventional exponential relaxation to memory-dominated power-law dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that hydrodynamic memory persists in the overdamped limit of colloidal diffusion, deriving a closed-form overdamped Langevin equation with memory and identifying the parameter controlling the crossover from exponential to power-law relaxation.
AI.motivation: Standard overdamped Langevin treatments of colloidal diffusion sacrifice convenience over realism: they eliminate velocity, omit inertia, and ignore the power-law memory arising from hydrodynamic memory effects. The authors aim to reconcile this gap by showing that hydrodynamic memory survives even in the colloid-inertialess limit.
AI.method: The authors identify the dimensionless parameter governing the crossover between early- and late-time dynamics and use it to derive, in closed form, an overdamped Langevin equation that retains hydrodynamic memory.
AI.result: The derived theory establishes a rigorous basis for the positional memory observed in high-resolution experiments. It predicts that hydrodynamic memory becomes more pronounced for smaller particles and under stronger external forcing, and it suggests experimental probes for the crossover from conventional exponential relaxation to memory-dominated power-law dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Hydrodynamic memory is not lost in the overdamped limit, and the closed-form overdamped Langevin equation provides a realistic theoretical framework for colloidal dynamics in a fluid.

title: Attosecond Charge Migration Induced by Core-Level Ionization: A Relativistic Real-Time Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory Perspective
summary: Core-ionization induced charge migration in molecular systems has been widely studied, but the influence of relativistic effects on such dynamics remains relatively unexplored from a relativistic theory perspective. This issue is particularly important because core orbitals exhibit strong scalar-relativistic and spin-orbit imprints, and these effects are further enhanced in heavy-element systems, where relativistic signatures also alter the valence orbitals. To address this, we formulate four-component Dirac-Coulomb and two-component atomic mean-field exact two-component (and non-relativistic) Hamiltonian approaches for studying charge migration within real-time time-dependent density functional theory. The time-dependent induced electric dipole moment is used as a marker of the characteristic charge-migration time scales. We apply the method to nitrosobenzene (N $1s$ electron removal), iodoacetylene (I $2p$ electron removal) and interhalogen series (I $2p$, Cl $2p$ electron removal). For iodoacetylene, the charge migration timescale is relatively insensitive to the choice of Hamiltonian but they show weak relativistic phase and amplitude modifications. However, it would be misleading to conclude that relativistic effects are generally unimportant. In interhalogen systems, we observe significant deviations between relativistic and non-relativistic dynamics. These results demonstrate that relativistic signatures in core-ionization-induced charge migration are not determined by heavy-atom core ionization alone, but by the relativistic sensitivity of the valence orbital manifold that drives core-hole screening and charge redistribution. Moreover, consistently across all systems, we observe a delay in the emergence of the relativistic imprints.

AI.tldr: This work develops four-component and two-component relativistic real-time TDDFT approaches to study relativistic effects on core-ionization-induced charge migration, showing that these effects depend on the relativistic sensitivity of the valence manifold rather than heavy-atom core ionization alone.
AI.motivation: Core-ionization-induced charge migration is well studied, but the role of relativistic effects remains largely unexplored from a relativistic theory perspective. This matters because core orbitals carry strong scalar-relativistic and spin-orbit signatures, enhanced in heavy elements where relativity also reshapes valence orbitals.
AI.method: The authors formulate four-component Dirac-Coulomb, two-component atomic mean-field exact two-component, and non-relativistic Hamiltonian approaches within real-time time-dependent density functional theory. The time-dependent induced electric dipole moment serves as a marker of charge-migration timescales. The method is applied to nitrosobenzene (N 1s removal), iodoacetylene (I 2p removal), and an interhalogen series (I 2p, Cl 2p removal).
AI.result: For iodoacetylene, the charge-migration timescale is largely insensitive to the Hamiltonian choice, though weak relativistic phase and amplitude modifications appear. In interhalogen systems, however, significant deviations between relativistic and non-relativistic dynamics are observed. Across all systems, a consistent delay in the emergence of relativistic imprints is found.
AI.conclusion: Relativistic signatures in core-ionization-induced charge migration are governed not solely by heavy-atom core ionization but by the relativistic sensitivity of the valence orbital manifold that drives core-hole screening and charge redistribution. Therefore, treating heavy-atom core ionization alone as sufficient to capture relativistic effects would be misleading.

title: Assessing the Reliability of Anomalous Hall Conductivity Extraction in GdAlSi
summary: We examine the different methods of extracting the anomalous Hall conductivity using SrRuO$_3$ and GdAlSi. For SrRuO$_3$, where the ordinary Hall background is well defined and the magnetoconductance is small, subtracting the ordinary Hall contribution either before or after conversion from resistivity to conductivity yields nearly identical anomalous Hall conductivities. In GdAlSi, in contrast, the transverse response does not exhibit clear saturation, and both low- and high-field regions can appear approximately linear. We show that different interpretations of these linear regions as the ordinary Hall background, together with the treatment of the measured longitudinal resistance in the resistivity-to-conductivity conversion, can produce completely different estimates of the anomalous Hall conductivity. We also examine whether the nonlinear Hall response can instead be described within an ordinary Hall framework without invoking an anomalous contribution. Our analysis provides practical cautions for extracting excess Hall contributions in quantum materials.

AI.tldr: A comparative case study of SrRuO3 and GdAlSi shows that anomalous Hall conductivity extraction is robust for SrRuO3 but highly method-dependent for GdAlSi, where ambiguous linear transverse responses and conversion choices can yield divergent results.
AI.motivation: Extracting the anomalous Hall conductivity (AHC) from measured Hall data requires separating it from the ordinary Hall background and converting resistivity to conductivity, but these steps can be ambiguous in materials without clear signatures. The paper aims to identify how these procedural choices affect the reliability of the extracted AHC.
AI.method: The authors compare two materials. For SrRuO3, where the ordinary Hall background is well defined and magnetoconductance is small, they test whether subtracting the ordinary Hall contribution before versus after the resistivity-to-conductivity conversion changes the AHC. For GdAlSi, where the transverse response lacks clear saturation and both low- and high-field regions appear approximately linear, they vary the interpretation of which linear region represents the ordinary Hall background and vary the treatment of the measured longitudinal resistance in the conversion. They also test whether the nonlinear Hall response can be explained purely within an ordinary Hall framework without an anomalous contribution.
AI.result: For SrRuO3, subtracting the ordinary Hall background before or after conversion yields nearly identical AHC values. For GdAlSi, different assignments of the linear regions as the ordinary background, combined with different treatments of the longitudinal resistance in the conversion, produce completely different estimates of the AHC. The nonlinear Hall response can also be described within an ordinary Hall framework without invoking an anomalous contribution.
