AI.conclusion: Extraction of excess (anomalous) Hall contributions in quantum materials is highly sensitive to the assumed ordinary Hall background and the resistivity-to-conductivity conversion procedure in cases lacking clear saturation or well-defined linearity, providing practical cautions for the field.

title: High-performance orbital-torque magnetic memory on the 300-mm platform
summary: Contemporary memory technologies are increasingly constrained by the fundamental trilemma of storage capacity, access latency, and power consumption. Among the emerging technologies, spin-orbit torque magnetic random-access memory (SOT-MRAM) shows promise to circumvent these challenges, owing to its fast switching dynamics and high endurance. However, the application of SOT-MRAM is hindered by the relatively low write and read efficiencies, resulting in a large bitcell area and an insufficient sensing margin. Meanwhile, the involvement of an ultrathin spin-source channel, typically within a few nanometers, imposes technological challenges for mass production. Here, we resolve these issues on a 300-mm wafer platform by exploiting the emerging orbital degree of freedom and the resultant orbital torque (OT) from the relatively thick Ti/W bilayer. In particular, OT memory nanodevices exhibit a giant tunnel magnetoresistance (TMR) of 182%, nanosecond-scale response, 1012 endurance, together with an enhanced switching efficiency (E_b/I_c), which consequently enables an ultra-low write energy of less than 0.1 pJ/bit. Our findings demonstrate that orbital angular momentum can be implemented for building energy-efficient MRAM devices, offering a practical pathway towards low-latency memory that is demanded for high-performance computing and AI applications.

AI.tldr: By exploiting orbital torque from a relatively thick Ti/W bilayer on a 300-mm wafer platform, the authors demonstrate OT-MRAM nanodevices with 182% TMR, nanosecond switching, 10^12 endurance, and sub-0.1 pJ/bit write energy.
AI.motivation: Contemporary memory technologies face a trilemma of storage capacity, access latency, and power consumption. SOT-MRAM is promising due to fast switching and high endurance, but suffers from low write/read efficiency (large bitcell area, insufficient sensing margin), and its ultrathin spin-source channel (a few nanometers) poses mass-production challenges.
AI.method: The authors exploit the orbital degree of freedom and the resulting orbital torque (OT) generated from a relatively thick Ti/W bilayer, fabricated on a 300-mm wafer platform, to build OT memory nanodevices.
AI.result: OT memory nanodevices achieve a giant tunnel magnetoresistance of 182%, nanosecond-scale response, 10^12 endurance, and enhanced switching efficiency (E_b/I_c), enabling ultra-low write energy below 0.1 pJ/bit.
AI.conclusion: Orbital angular momentum can be implemented to build energy-efficient MRAM devices, offering a practical pathway toward low-latency memory demanded by high-performance computing and AI applications.

title: A consistent and conservative Phase-Field method for compressible multiphase flows with the six-equation model
summary: In the present study, the consistent and conservative Phase-Field method is extended to the six-equation model for compressible multiphase flows. Based solely on the conservation laws and the second law of thermodynamics, the six-equation model with the Phase-Field mechanism is first derived. In addition to satisfying Galilean invariance and consistency of reduction, the model is general to admit an arbitrary number of phases with different formulations of the Phase-Field mechanism. The isobaric closure by the pressure relaxation and the incompressible limit of the proposed model are analyzed. The derivation and analysis identify additional terms arising from the Phase-Field mechanism, which are absent from previous studies. The consistent and conservative numerical approach is adapted to the proposed six-equation model with moderate modifications, retaining the interfacial equilibrium condition, conservation, and flexibility and robustness of incorporating different formulations of the Phase-Field mechanism with bound preservation. As the new component of solving the six-equation model, both the pressure and pressure-temperature relaxations are theoretically analyzed in a general multiphase setup, with a proof of the existence and uniqueness of a thermodynamically admissible solution for these two relaxations. Various two-phase compressible flow benchmarks are performed to demonstrate the method, and good agreement with exact solutions is achieved.

AI.tldr: This paper extends a consistent and conservative Phase-Field method to the six-equation model for compressible multiphase flows, deriving the model from conservation laws and the second law of thermodynamics, analyzing pressure and pressure-temperature relaxations, and validating it on two-phase benchmark cases.
AI.motivation: The six-equation model for compressible multiphase flows needs a formulation that is simultaneously consistent, conservative, Galilean-invariant, reduction-consistent, and generalizable to an arbitrary number of phases with different Phase-Field mechanisms. Previous studies missed additional terms arising from the Phase-Field mechanism, and the pressure and pressure-temperature relaxations lacked a general theoretical treatment with guarantees of well-posedness.
AI.method: The six-equation model with the Phase-Field mechanism is derived solely from conservation laws and the second law of thermodynamics. The isobaric closure via pressure relaxation and the incompressible limit are analyzed. The consistent and conservative numerical approach is adapted to the proposed model with moderate modifications, preserving interfacial equilibrium, conservation, flexibility/robustness, bound preservation, and support for multiple Phase-Field formulations. Both pressure and pressure-temperature relaxations are theoretically analyzed in a general multiphase setup.
AI.result: The derivation is general for an arbitrary number of phases and admits different Phase-Field formulations while satisfying Galilean invariance and consistency of reduction. Additional terms arising from the Phase-Field mechanism, absent in prior work, are identified. Existence and uniqueness of a thermodynamically admissible solution are proven for both the pressure and pressure-temperature relaxations. Two-phase compressible flow benchmarks show good agreement with exact solutions.
AI.conclusion: The extended consistent and conservative Phase-Field method yields a general, well-posed six-equation model for compressible multiphase flows, with provable well-posedness of its relaxations and accurate numerical results, providing a robust framework for multiphase simulation with different Phase-Field mechanisms.

title: Experimental assessment of the Wiedemann-Franz law in thin metal films using thermoreflectance and electrical measurements
summary: Accurate thermal properties of metal thin films are essential for microelectronic thermal modeling and for interpreting thermoreflectance measurements when signals are sensitive to film thermal transport. In practice, film thermal conductivity is commonly inferred from electrical resistivity via the Wiedemann-Franz (WF) law with the Sommerfeld-Lorenz number L_0, neglecting phonon contributions and microstructure-dependent scattering. Here, we combine square-pulsed source (SPS) thermoreflectance with van der Pauw measurements to characterize thermal and electrical transport in Al, Ti, and Ta thin films prepared by thermal evaporation, e-beam evaporation, and magnetron sputtering. SPS measurements from 80 to 300 K yield the film thermal conductivity k_m and volumetric heat capacity C_m, with C_m agreeing with bulk values within +/-8%. Compared with WF-based estimates using L_0 and a modeled resistivity, \r{ho}_model (T)=\r{ho}_bulk (T)+\r{ho}_0, k_m deviates by 5-20% for Al and Ti and up to 40% for sputtered Ta at 300 K. While the smaller deviations are comparable to experimental uncertainty, the large mismatch for Ta demonstrates the limitation of applying the bulk L_0 to highly resistive metal films. Apparent Lorenz numbers L_app=k_m \r{ho}_meas/T from 150 to 300 K further reveal that deposition-induced disorder, grain-boundary scattering, and possible phase-related effects can modify the correlation between heat and charge transport in thin metal films. These results clarify the applicability of the WF law to deposited metal thin films and offer practical guidance for thermal modeling and thermoreflectance analysis.

AI.tldr: This work combines square-pulsed source (SPS) thermoreflectance with van der Pauw measurements to characterize thermal and electrical transport in Al, Ti, and Ta thin films, testing the validity of the Wiedemann-Franz (WF) law for metal thin films. Film thermal conductivity k_m and volumetric heat capacity C_m were extracted from 80 to 300 K, revealing that WF-based estimates deviate by 5-20% for Al and Ti and up to 40% for sputtered Ta at 300 K.
AI.motivation: Accurate thermal properties of metal thin films are essential for microelectronic thermal modeling and for interpreting thermoreflectance measurements. In practice, film thermal conductivity is commonly inferred from electrical resistivity via the Wiedemann-Franz (WF) law with the Sommerfeld-Lorenz number L_0, neglecting phonon contributions and microstructure-dependent scattering. The applicability of this assumption to deposited metal thin films needs clarification.
AI.method: The authors combine square-pulsed source (SPS) thermoreflectance with van der Pauw electrical measurements to characterize thermal and electrical transport in Al, Ti, and Ta thin films prepared by thermal evaporation, e-beam evaporation, and magnetron sputtering. SPS measurements from 80 to 300 K yield film thermal conductivity k_m and volumetric heat capacity C_m, which are compared with WF-based estimates using L_0 and a modeled resistivity, rho_model(T) = rho_bulk(T) + rho_0. Apparent Lorenz numbers L_app = k_m * rho_meas / T are extracted from 150 to 300 K.
AI.result: The measured volumetric heat capacity C_m agrees with bulk values within +/-8%. The large deviation for sputtered Ta shows that applying the bulk Sommerfeld-Lorenz number L_0 to highly resistive metal films is unreliable, whereas Al and Ti deviations are comparable to experimental uncertainty. These results clarify the applicability of the WF law to deposited metal thin films and offer practical guidance for thermal modeling and thermoreflectance analysis.

title: Second-Order Rayleigh-Schrödinger Perturbation Theory for the GRASP2018 Package: Three-Particle Feynman Diagram Contribution to Core-Valence Correlations
summary: In order to ascertain the precise atomic characteristics, it is important to incorporate a wide range of electron correlations in the computational analysis. However, it is important to note that undertaking such studies will result in substantial increases of the CSF expansions. The present publication, as well as the series of articles that have been published by G. Gaigalas, P. Rynkun, and L. Kitovienė, are dedicated to the analysis and resolution of the problem in question. In this series, a method was developed based on second-order perturbation theory to identify the most important core-valence, core, core-core, and valence-valence correlations. The method under discussion is based on a combination of the relativistic configuration interaction method and the stationary second-order Rayleigh-Schrödinger many-body perturbation theory in an irreducible tensorial form. In this study, the method is further expanded to encompass additional core-valence electron correlations of the third and fourth types. Conversely, the correlations that are not encompassed by perturbation theory are addressed in a conventional manner. This method can be used to calculate the properties of an atom or ion with any number of valence and core electrons. As an example of its application, the atomic calculations of the energy structure and lifetime for Ne II are presented.

AI.tldr: An extended second-order perturbation-theory method selects the dominant electron correlations (including additional core-valence types III and IV) to keep configuration-interaction expansions tractable, demonstrated on Ne II energy structure and lifetimes.
AI.motivation: Accurate atomic properties require incorporating a wide range of electron correlations, but doing so causes a substantial (combinatorial) growth of configuration state function (CSF) expansions, making the computations prohibitively large. A systematic way to identify only the essential correlation contributions is needed.
AI.method: The approach combines the relativistic configuration interaction (RCI) method with stationary second-order Rayleigh-Schrödinger many-body perturbation theory (MBPT) in an irreducible tensorial form. Building on prior work by Gaigalas, Rynkun, and Kitovienė that targeted core-valence, core, core-core, and valence-valence correlations, the method is extended here to include additional core-valence correlations of the third and fourth types. Correlations not captured by perturbation theory are treated conventionally. The scheme is general, applicable to atoms/ions with arbitrary numbers of valence and core electrons.
AI.result: The extended method was applied to atomic calculations of the energy structure and lifetimes for Ne II, yielding the target properties while managing CSF expansion size.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating a refined set of perturbatively selected electron correlations allows accurate atomic structure and lifetime calculations without uncontrolled CSF expansion growth, and the approach generalizes to systems with any number of valence and core electrons.

title: Brownian motion with geometry-dependent hydrodynamic memory
summary: Micron-sized particles moving through a fluid are subject to viscous resistance and thermal fluctuations. Beyond steady Stokes friction, colloids also exhibit hydrodynamic memory effects arising from conservation laws of the surrounding fluid. Although fluid-flow problems in complex geometries and confinements are often highly involved, numerical or approximate solutions can be obtained; translating these solutions into closed-form equations of motion for individual colloids, however, is rarely possible. Here, we develop a theoretical framework that provides both underdamped and overdamped colloidal dynamics from the solution of an arbitrary flow problem: (i) Using the Lorentz reciprocal theorem, we express the colloidal equation of motion in terms of the geometry's Green's function and the fluid-flow profile. This formulation yields both the corresponding Stokes drag as well as a Basset-like hydrodynamic memory contribution. (ii) As colloid inertia is often negligible, we furthermore derive the corresponding overdamped (colloid-inertia-less) limit, which inherits the Stokes and Basset-like resistances and additionally gives rise to a spurious drift. We propose applications of this framework to passive and active particles subject to involved confinements and problem geometries.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a general theoretical framework to derive closed-form underdamped and overdamped equations of motion for colloids in arbitrary flow geometries, expressing Stokes drag, Basset-like memory, and a spurious drift via the Lorentz reciprocal theorem and the geometry's Green's function.
AI.motivation: Micron-sized colloids in fluids experience viscous resistance, thermal fluctuations, and hydrodynamic memory from fluid conservation laws. While flow problems in complex or confined geometries can be solved numerically or approximately, converting those solutions into closed-form equations of motion for individual colloids is rarely feasible, motivating a general method to bridge this gap.
AI.method: (i) Apply the Lorentz reciprocal theorem to express the colloidal equation of motion in terms of the geometry's Green's function and the fluid-flow profile, yielding both the Stokes drag and a Basset-like hydrodynamic memory term. (ii) Derive the overdamped (colloid-inertia-less) limit, which retains the Stokes and Basset-like resistances and additionally produces a spurious drift.
AI.result: A unified framework furnishing both underdamped and overdamped colloidal dynamics from the solution of an arbitrary flow problem, capturing Stokes drag, Basset-like memory, and spurious drift in closed form.
AI.conclusion: The framework is proposed for application to passive and active particles under involved confinements and problem geometries.

title: On-Water Surface Catalysis: From Hydrogen Bonding to Charge-Transfer Activation
summary:
On-water catalysis accelerates reactions between poorly soluble organic substrates in aqueous suspensions, but its molecular origin remains debated. This Account argues that hydrogen bonding and proton transfer can both enhance charge-transfer stabilization between the organic reactants. Hydrogen bonds from surface water polarize the reacting complex, whereas protonation can perturb the same donor-acceptor interaction more strongly without requiring identical reaction pathways.
  We connect simulations of the water/vapor interface, finite-temperature cycloaddition studies, and energy decomposition analysis based on absolutely localized molecular orbitals. Dangling OH groups establish reactive contacts, but an increased transition-state hydrogen-bond count alone does not explain activation. Electronic analysis instead identified hydration-enhanced charge-transfer stabilization between organic partners by approximately 30%. Comparisons of related dienophiles, a protonated limiting model, and oxygen/sulfur substitution link substrate-dependent electronic response to hydration and bond formation.
  A hydration-induced charge-transfer response metric provides a testable molecular hypothesis, not a standalone measure of catalytic acceleration. Activation depends on differential stabilization of reactant and transition-state ensembles. Increasing the accessible reactive interface can amplify this local mechanism without requiring exceptionally strong additional electric fields, connecting conventional on-water chemistry with selected microdroplet reactions while distinguishing adsorption, concentration, and intrinsic molecular activation.

AI.tldr: This Account proposes that on-water catalysis arises from hydrogen bonding and proton transfer enhancing charge-transfer (CT) stabilization between poorly soluble organic reactants, identified via ALMO-based energy decomposition analysis of interfacial simulations.
AI.motivation: The molecular origin of on-water catalysis—accelerated reactions between poorly soluble organic substrates in aqueous suspensions—remains debated. Existing explanations based on interfacial dangling OH groups and increased transition-state hydrogen-bond counts are insufficient to account for the observed activation.
AI.method: The authors combine simulations of the water/vapor interface, finite-temperature cycloaddition studies, and energy decomposition analysis based on absolutely localized molecular orbitals (ALMO-EDA), and compare related dienophiles, a protonated limiting model, and oxygen/sulfur substitution.
AI.result: Dangling OH groups establish reactive contacts, but an increased transition-state hydrogen-bond count alone does not explain activation. Electronic analysis reveals hydration-enhanced charge-transfer stabilization between organic partners of approximately 30%. Comparisons across substrates link substrate-dependent electronic response to hydration and bond formation.
AI.conclusion: A hydration-induced charge-transfer response metric offers a testable molecular hypothesis rather than a standalone measure of catalytic acceleration. Activation depends on differential stabilization of reactant versus transition-state ensembles; enlarging the accessible reactive interface can amplify this local mechanism without exceptionally strong additional electric fields, connecting conventional on-water chemistry with selected microdroplet reactions while distinguishing adsorption, concentration, and intrinsic molecular activation.

title: Optical investigation of the electronic structure of a ferromagnetic Weyl semimetal CeAlSi
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, SM: 5 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables
summary: To investigate electronic states during the ferromagnetic transition in a magnetic Weyl semimetal CeAlSi, we measured temperature-dependent optical conductivity [$σ_1(ω)$] spectra and compared them with DFT+DMFT band calculations. The $σ_1(ω)$ spectrum did not change significantly across the ferromagnetic ordering temperature ($T_C$), suggesting that the Ce 4f states are almost localized. DFT+DMFT calculations with almost localized Ce 4f states successfully reproduced the spectral shape and the unchanged $σ_1(ω)$ spectra across $T_C$. The dynamic effective mass evaluated from the extended Drude model is very small, which DFT+DMFT calculations also reproduce, but the scattering probability at even lower temperatures suggests ferromagnetic fluctuations. These results suggest that the interaction intensity between the Weyl fermions and Ce 4f states is very weak, as reproduced by DFT+DMFT calculations.

AI.tldr: Optical conductivity spectra and DFT+DMFT calculations on the magnetic Weyl semimetal CeAlSi show that the Ce 4f states remain almost localized through the ferromagnetic transition, with weak coupling between Weyl fermions and Ce 4f states.
AI.motivation: To investigate the electronic states during the ferromagnetic transition in the magnetic Weyl semimetal CeAlSi.
AI.method: Temperature-dependent optical conductivity [σ1(ω)] spectra were measured and compared with DFT+DMFT band calculations. The dynamic effective mass was evaluated using the extended Drude model.
AI.result: The σ1(ω) spectrum shows no significant change across the ferromagnetic ordering temperature TC, indicating nearly localized Ce 4f states. DFT+DMFT calculations with almost localized Ce 4f states reproduce both the spectral shape and the unchanged σ1(ω) across TC. The dynamic effective mass is very small, also reproduced by DFT+DMFT, while the scattering probability at lower temperatures suggests ferromagnetic fluctuations.
AI.conclusion: The interaction intensity between Weyl fermions and Ce 4f states is very weak, as reproduced by DFT+DMFT calculations.

title: Disentangling Strain and Ti3+ Contributions to the Anomalous Hall Effect in Epitaxial RuO2 Films
summary: The anomalous Hall effect (AHE) reported in epitaxial RuO2/TiO2 has been attributed to a strain-stabilized magnetic state, but strain can be entangled with Ru-Ti intermixing and interfacial charge redistribution, which can produce Ti3+ and potentially localized moments. Here, we disentangle these contributions using Ti-alloyed RuO2 heterostructures in which abundant Ti3+ states are retained while epitaxial strain is independently changed. The strained and relaxed films have nearly identical Ti/Ru compositions and comparable Ti3+ fractions, yet a pronounced nonlinear AHE appears only in the coherently strained film, while the relaxed heterostructure exhibits an almost linear Hall response. Spectroscopic ellipsometry further shows that the AHE-active strained state is accompanied by a reconstruction of the itinerant electronic response, including enhanced metallicity and longer carrier relaxation times. These results show that Ti3+ formation alone is insufficient to generate the anomalous Hall state and identify epitaxial strain, through its modification of the itinerant RuO2 electronic structure, as the dominant control parameter.

AI.tldr: Epitaxial strain, not Ti3+-related localized moments, is shown to be the dominant control parameter for the anomalous Hall effect in Ti-alloyed RuO2 heterostructures.
AI.motivation: The anomalous Hall effect in epitaxial RuO2/TiO2 has been attributed to a strain-stabilized magnetic state, but strain is often entangled with Ru-Ti intermixing and interfacial charge redistribution that can generate Ti3+ and localized moments, leaving the true origin unclear.
AI.method: Ti-alloyed RuO2 heterostructures were used to decouple strain from Ti3+ formation: strained and relaxed films with nearly identical Ti/Ru compositions and comparable Ti3+ fractions were compared via Hall transport measurements and spectroscopic ellipsometry.
AI.result: A pronounced nonlinear AHE appears only in the coherently strained film, whereas the relaxed heterostructure shows an almost linear Hall response. The AHE-active strained state exhibits reconstructed itinerant electronic response, including enhanced metallicity and longer carrier relaxation times.
AI.conclusion: Ti3+ formation alone is insufficient to generate the anomalous Hall state; epitaxial strain, through its modification of the itinerant RuO2 electronic structure, is the dominant control parameter.

title: Improved lattice Boltzmann method for conjugate magnetohydrodynamic simulations
comment: The first conjugate MHD simulations by an improved LBM
summary: In the simulation of conjugate magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) flows, where a moving conducting fluid dynamically interacts with bounding conducting walls under the influence of an externally imposed magnetic field, resolving the electrical conductivity transition across the fluid-solid interface introduces significant numerical challenges. In problems with high magnetic Reynolds numbers, it is required to solve the full magnetic induction formulation that has a curl-of-curl term for the magnetic diffusion, which is simplified to a divergence term in the original vector-valued lattice Boltzmann method (LBM). The resulting LBM scheme is valid for simulating fluid domains with a constant conductivity where its bounding solid walls are modelled using appropriate boundary conditions. The current study shows that this scheme is also valid for two-dimensional conjugate MHD simulations where the magnetic field component with non-zero gradients is perpendicular to the conductivity gradient. For general conjugate MHD simulations, we improve the LBM scheme by considering the difference between the curl-of-curl term and the simplified divergence form, which is treated as a source term in the LBM evolution algorithm and computed using an efficient LBM discretisation scheme. The improved LBM scheme automatically satisfies the required conjugate constraints at the fluid-solid interface as a volume integral inside two adjacent boundary layers. The accuracy of the improved LBM scheme is verified by piecewise analytical solutions in benchmark problems with an abrupt conductivity jump across the fluid-solid interface.

AI.tldr: An improved vector-valued lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) is proposed for conjugate MHD flows with conductivity jumps across fluid-solid interfaces, by adding the discarded curl-of-curl correction as a source term.
AI.motivation: In conjugate MHD simulations, resolving the electrical conductivity transition across fluid-solid interfaces is numerically challenging. At high magnetic Reynolds numbers, the full magnetic induction formulation with a curl-of-curl diffusion term must be solved, but the original vector-valued LBM simplifies this to a divergence term, which is only valid for constant-conductivity domains with boundary conditions on walls. A scheme capable of handling general conductivity gradients and conjugate interfaces is needed.
AI.method: The study first demonstrates that the original simplified LBM scheme is valid for 2D conjugate MHD when the magnetic field component with non-zero gradients is perpendicular to the conductivity gradient. For general conjugate MHD, the scheme is improved by retaining the difference between the curl-of-curl term and its simplified divergence form, treating it as a source term in the LBM evolution algorithm and computing it with an efficient LBM discretisation. The improved scheme automatically enforces the conjugate constraints at the fluid-solid interface as a volume integral inside two adjacent boundary layers.
AI.result: Piecewise analytical solutions in benchmark problems featuring an abrupt conductivity jump across the fluid-solid interface verify the accuracy of the improved LBM scheme.
AI.conclusion: The improved vector-valued LBM enables accurate conjugate MHD simulations with conductivity discontinuities, extending the scheme's validity beyond constant-conductivity domains and automatically satisfying interface conjugate constraints.

title: Unconventional linear transverse exciton transport in valley-layer coupling two-dimensional materials
summary: Valley-layer coupling (VLC) two-dimensional (2D) materials define a distinct class of quantum systems in which valleys are related by crystal, rather than time-reversal ($\mathcal{T}$) symmetry, enabling gate-controlled valley-contrasted layer polarization. Here we extend this concept to excitons. Using TiSiCo as a prototype VLC material, we show that a perpendicular electric field $E_{\perp}$ controls exciton- dispersion anisotropy and thereby generates unconventional linear transverse exciton transport in both monolayer and twisted bilayer structures. In the monolayer, this response is characterized by anisotropy-induced transverse conductivities, arising from the antisymmetric combination of diagonal elements in the conductivity tensor and strongly tunable by $E_{\perp}$. In the twisted bilayer, symmetry additionally permits transverse responses from the symmetric part of the conductivity tensor. Since intralayer excitons in different layers are connected by the Förster coupling, these symmetric and antisymmetric responses coexist and compete with the recently proposed $\mathcal{T}$-even layer Hall and Nernst exciton counterflow. This interplay is highly tunable by twisted angle, temperature, and the direction of the in-plane driving force, providing a route to disentangle distinct transverse exciton transport signals experimentally. Our results establish $E_{\perp}$ as a powerful knob for controlling exciton transport via VLC and identify VLC 2D materials as a promising platform for engineered excitonic phenomena.

AI.tldr: This work extends valley-layer coupling (VLC) from charge carriers to excitons in TiSiCo, showing that a perpendicular electric field controls exciton dispersion anisotropy and enables unconventional transverse exciton transport in monolayer and twisted bilayer, with competing symmetric/antisymmetric responses tunable by twist angle, temperature, and drive direction.
AI.motivation: VLC 2D materials form a distinct class of quantum systems where valleys are related by crystal rather than time-reversal symmetry, enabling gate-controlled valley-contrasted layer polarization. The authors aim to extend this concept from the established charge-carrier regime to excitons, which could open new routes for controlling excitonic transport via an external electric field.
AI.method: Using TiSiCo as a prototype VLC material, they analyze exciton dispersion under a perpendicular electric field E⊥ in monolayer and twisted bilayer structures. In the monolayer they derive anisotropy-induced transverse conductivities from the antisymmetric combination of diagonal conductivity-tensor elements. In the twisted bilayer they additionally include transverse responses from the symmetric part of the conductivity tensor, together with the Förster coupling connecting intralayer excitons in different layers, and examine the competition with T-even layer Hall and Nernst exciton counterflow.
AI.result: A perpendicular electric field E⊥ controls exciton dispersion anisotropy and generates linear transverse exciton transport. In the monolayer, transverse conductivities arise from the antisymmetric combination of diagonal tensor elements and are strongly tunable by E⊥. In the twisted bilayer, symmetry additionally allows symmetric-part transverse responses; these coexist and compete with the T-even layer Hall and Nernst exciton counterflow. The interplay is highly tunable by twist angle, temperature, and in-plane driving-force direction.
AI.conclusion: E⊥ acts as a powerful knob for controlling exciton transport via VLC. The distinct, competing transverse responses provide a route to experimentally disentangle different transport signals, and VLC 2D materials are identified as a promising platform for engineered excitonic phenomena.

title: Improved systematic uncertainty evaluation of the $^{171}$Yb optical lattice clock NMIJ-Yb1 with uncertainty of $2.6\times10^{-17}$
summary: We report a systematic uncertainty evaluation of the $^{171}$Yb optical lattice clock NMIJ-Yb1 (NMIJ: National Metrology Institute of Japan) with a fractional frequency uncertainty of $2.6\times10^{-17}$, improved by a factor of 3.8 compared with our previous uncertainty. The uncertainty of the lattice light shift is reduced to $1.6\times10^{-17}$ by preparing axially sideband-cooled atoms in a shallow optical lattice. Different models to calculate the lattice light shift are compared, taking account of possible model-dependent biases due to the treatment of the radial motion of atoms trapped in the optical lattice. The uncertainty of the blackbody radiation shift reaches $7.0\times10^{-18}$ by measuring the radiative temperature at the position of atoms with an in-vacuum temperature sensor. We also demonstrate the nearly continuous operation of NMIJ-Yb1 with an uptime of 91.3 $\%$ for 10 days, showing the potential for future improvement of the calibration uncertainty of International Atomic Time.

AI.tldr: Systematic uncertainty of the NMIJ-Yb1 optical lattice clock is reduced to a fractional frequency uncertainty of 2.6×10⁻¹⁷ (a factor of 3.8 improvement), with lattice light shift and blackbody radiation shift evaluated at 1.6×10⁻¹⁷ and 7.0×10⁻¹⁸, and 91.3% uptime demonstrated over 10 days.
AI.motivation: To improve the frequency uncertainty of the NMIJ-Yb1 optical lattice clock, which is important for applications such as contributing to International Atomic Time calibration.
AI.method: Evaluation of systematic shifts: prepare axially sideband-cooled atoms in a shallow optical lattice to reduce the lattice light shift; compare different models for calculating the lattice light shift considering model-dependent biases from radial atomic motion; measure radiative temperature at the atoms' position using an in-vacuum temperature sensor for the blackbody radiation shift; and demonstrate continuous operation.
AI.result: Fractional frequency uncertainty of 2.6×10⁻¹⁷, improved by a factor of 3.8 over previous work. Lattice light shift uncertainty reduced to 1.6×10⁻¹⁷; blackbody radiation shift uncertainty reached 7.0×10⁻¹⁸; nearly continuous operation with 91.3% uptime over 10 days.
AI.conclusion: The improved uncertainty and high uptime show potential for future enhancement of the calibration uncertainty of International Atomic Time.

title: Activity-induced emergent flatness, instabilities and pattern formation in fluid membranes
summary: We show that microscopically inversion-asymmetric, permeable active fluid membranes are statistically flat and effectively inversion-symmetric at large scales. Their fluctuations are governed by an asymptotically exact linear hydrodynamic equation giving orientational long-range order and positional quasi-long-range order. At intermediate scales, their dynamics is described by a Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation with spatially long-range noise, producing rough membranes with short-range translational and long-range orientational order described by exactly known scaling exponents. Active stresses can destabilize the membrane at long wavelengths, while sufficiently strong active permeation flow can drive finite-wavevector instabilities and pattern formation. These results reveal a novel activity-driven route to the destruction of flat fluid membranes.

AI.tldr: Permeable, inversion-asymmetric active fluid membranes are statistically flat and effectively inversion-symmetric at large scales, showing quasi-long-range positional and long-range orientational order.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates how activity and membrane permeability (microscopic inversion asymmetry) affect the statistical mechanics and stability of fluid membranes.
AI.method: Hydrodynamic analysis of active fluid membranes, deriving an asymptotically exact linear hydrodynamic equation at large scales and a Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation with spatially long-range noise at intermediate scales, using known scaling exponents.
AI.result: Large-scale fluctuations obey the linear hydrodynamic equation, yielding orientational long-range order and positional quasi-long-range order. At intermediate scales, KPZ dynamics with long-range noise produces rough membranes with short-range translational and long-range orientational order. Active stresses can destabilize the membrane at long wavelengths, while strong active permeation flow can induce finite-wavevector instabilities and pattern formation.
AI.conclusion: These findings reveal a novel activity-driven mechanism for the destruction of flat fluid membranes.

title: Variational computation of anharmonic ground and excited vibrational eigenstates using bound Quartic Force Fields: Application with MCTDH and ElVibRot
summary: In this work we introduce the use of Quartic Force fields (QFF) potential expansions in the context of variational calculations. Such potentials are commonly employed in molecular Vibrational Second-Order Perturbation Theory (VPT2) studies, for which equations explicitly dependent on the QFF parameters exist. However, QFF are unbound potentials for more or less large displacements from the reference point and, most of the time, this prevents their use in conjunction with variational wavepacket-based calculations. In this work, we propose a general correction to QFFs and introduce a fully automated numerical approach to avoid their unbound character. Our corrected potentials, bound QFF (bQFF), do not exhibit appreciable modification of the local topography around the region of interest for infrared spectroscopy. As a consequence of this, we can affirm that the vibrational eigenstructure (eigenvalues, eigenstates) remains essentially unaltered by our correction. To illustrate their numerical stability, we have interfaced our bQFF routines in combination with to two well-established quantum simulation software packages MCTDH and \textsc{ElVibRot} which feature variational approaches. More specifically, our bQFFs are separable and hence directly expressible as MCTDH operators. Furthermore, concerning the size of our bQFF expansion, we show that it is possible to tensor-decompose our bQFF in Canonical Polyadic form (CP-bQFF). We use the Monte Carlo Canonical Polyadic decomposition algorithm for this. CP-bQFF results are virtually identical to uncompressed bQFF, but the computational efficiency is largely improved. Our approach paves the way for the automated variational study of anharmonic eigenstates in molecular systems within the reach of QFF-based potentials, using either time-dependent or time-independent schemes.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "bound Quartic Force Fields" (bQFF), a corrected QFF potential that removes the unbound character of standard QFFs, enabling their use in variational (time-dependent and time-independent) vibrational calculations. The correction preserves the local topography and eigenstructure while allowing separability into MCTDH operators and Canonical Polyadic tensor decomposition for improved efficiency.
AI.motivation: Quartic Force Fields (QFFs) are widely used in VPT2 studies due to equations explicitly dependent on QFF parameters. However, QFFs are unbound potentials for large displacements from the reference point, which typically prevents their use in variational wavepacket-based calculations. This work aims to make QFF potentials usable within variational frameworks.
AI.method: The authors propose a general correction to QFFs and a fully automated numerical approach to eliminate their unbound character, yielding "bound QFF" (bQFF). The bQFF is separable and directly expressible as MCTDH operators. They interface bQFF routines with two variational quantum simulation software packages (MCTDH and ElVibRot). Additionally, they tensor-decompose the bQFF into Canonical Polyadic form (CP-bQFF) using the Monte Carlo Canonical Polyadic decomposition algorithm.
AI.result: The corrected bQFF potentials show no appreciable modification of the local topography around the infrared spectroscopy region of interest, so the vibrational eigenstructure (eigenvalues, eigenstates) remains essentially unaltered. The bQFF routines demonstrate numerical stability when interfaced with MCTDH and ElVibRot. CP-bQFF results are virtually identical to uncompressed bQFF, with largely improved computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables automated variational study of anharmonic eigenstates in molecular systems within the reach of QFF-based potentials, using either time-dependent or time-independent schemes. This paves the way for broader application of QFF potentials in variational vibrational calculations.

title: Orbital-Induced Peierls Transitions: How Orbitals Orchestrate Lattice Instability
summary: The Peierls transition is typically regarded as a phenomenon inherent to one-dimensional (1D) materials. However, orbital degrees of freedom can induce this instability even in higher dimensions. Two mechanisms are primarily responsible. First, the anisotropic shape of $p$ and $d$ orbitals can lead to effective "1D-zation" of the electronic spectrum. Second, orbital degrees of freedom can lift band degeneracy by shifting bands relative to each other via the local or band Jahn-Teller effect, thereby affecting the nesting of the Fermi surface. The orbital-induced Peierls effect is most commonly observed when ligand octahedra surrounding transition metals share edges, and less frequently in face-sharing geometries. In this review, we discuss the underlying physical mechanisms, the materials in which this phenomenon occurs, the characteristics of the high-temperature undistorted phase, and the role of local effects such as the formation of molecular orbitals.

AI.tldr: The review discusses how orbital degrees of freedom can induce the Peierls transition even beyond 1D materials, through effective "1D-zation" of the electronic spectrum and Jahn-Teller-driven band degeneracy lifting that alters Fermi surface nesting.
AI.motivation: The Peierls transition is conventionally viewed as a 1D phenomenon, but orbital degrees of freedom can trigger this instability in higher-dimensional systems, motivating a unified review of the mechanisms and materials involved.
AI.method: Review of the physical mechanisms (orbital-shaped-induced effective 1D-zation and local/band Jahn-Teller effects lifting band degeneracy and modifying Fermi surface nesting), the materials exhibiting the effect, the properties of the high-temperature undistorted phase, and local effects such as molecular orbital formation.
AI.result: The orbital-induced Peierls effect is most commonly observed with edge-sharing ligand octahedra around transition metals, and less frequently in face-sharing geometries.
AI.conclusion: Orbital degrees of freedom provide a route to Peierls-type instabilities in higher dimensions, and their interplay with geometry (edge- vs face-sharing octahedra) and local molecular-orbital effects governs where and how the phenomenon appears.

title: Braided endovascular implants for intracranial aneurysms: mechanics, hemodynamics, and clinical translation
summary: Endovascular implants prevent intracranial aneurysm rupture by altering the mechanical and hemodynamic environment at the aneurysm neck. Yet many in silico workflows prescribe or reconstruct the post-deployment geometry before computing flow, leaving unresolved the mechanics that create the clinically relevant interface. Here we review braided intraluminal flow diverters, intrasaccular devices, and emerging flow-disruption concepts across deployment mechanics, inter-wire and wire-wall contact, superelasticity, wall apposition, pore geometry, computational fluid dynamics, and fluid-structure interaction. We connect these modeling choices to neck coverage, malapposition, migration, deformation, and durability, and distinguish established evidence from mechanistic inference and prospective hypotheses. We argue that model fidelity should match the clinical question: prescribed or fast placement may support screening, whereas questions of coverage, apposition, compaction, and migration benefit from mechanically plausible deployment states. An interface-resolved mechanics-to-flow framework, supported by measurable validation targets and standardized reporting, could improve device design and enable more reliable patient-specific treatment planning.

AI.tldr: This review examines computational modeling of endovascular aneurysm implants (braided flow diverters, intrasaccular devices, flow-disruption concepts), arguing that deployment mechanics are typically neglected in silico workflows and that an interface-resolved mechanics-to-flow framework with measurable validation and standardized reporting is needed.
AI.motivation: Endovascular implants prevent intracranial aneurysm rupture by modifying the mechanical and hemodynamic environment at the aneurysm neck. However, many in silico workflows prescribe or reconstruct post-deployment geometry before computing flow, leaving unresolved the mechanics that generate the clinically relevant neck interface. This gap motivates a review of how modeling choices affect clinically meaningful outcomes.
AI.method: The authors review braided intraluminal flow diverters, intrasaccular devices, and emerging flow-disruption concepts across multiple modeling domains: deployment mechanics, inter-wire and wire-wall contact, superelasticity, wall apposition, pore geometry, computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and fluid-structure interaction (FSI). They link these modeling choices to neck coverage, malapposition, migration, deformation, and durability, distinguishing established evidence from mechanistic inference and prospective hypotheses.
AI.result: The review finds that model fidelity should be matched to the clinical question: prescribed or fast placement may be adequate for screening purposes, whereas questions of coverage, apposition, compaction, and migration require mechanically plausible deployment states. Neglecting deployment mechanics limits the reliability of hemodynamic predictions at the aneurysm neck.
AI.conclusion: An interface-resolved mechanics-to-flow framework, supported by measurable validation targets and standardized reporting, could improve device design and enable more reliable patient-specific treatment planning for intracranial aneurysm intervention.

title: Fully differentiable framework for inverse identification of geometry and material parameters with application to determining stress-free configuration of soft tissues
summary: Medical images of soft tissues typically depict loaded configurations rather than true unloaded (stress-free) states, which can bias biomechanical simulations and inverse material identification. A gradient-based inverse finite element framework is presented that jointly reconstructs an effective unloaded reference geometry and estimates hyperelastic material parameters from two or more observed deformed configurations. The formulation is fully differentiable and leverages exact end-to-end gradients to enable unified, simultaneous optimization of geometry and constitutive parameters. The objective function combines a nodal-position misfit with a deformation-gradient-based mismatch term, improving robustness under large deformations. Benchmark studies quantify the influence of loading diversity and observation count and demonstrate reduced sensitivity to poor material initialization. Finally, application to an MRI-derived breast model shows accurate recovery of the unloaded configuration and constitutive parameters from multiple gravity-loaded states. The framework provides a unified and scalable tool for inverse biomechanics with potential applications in personalized modeling, elastography, and surgical planning.

AI.tldr: A fully differentiable, gradient-based inverse finite element framework jointly reconstructs the unloaded reference geometry and estimates hyperelastic material parameters from multiple observed deformed configurations, validated on benchmarks and an MRI-derived breast model.
AI.motivation: Medical images of soft tissues typically capture loaded configurations rather than true unloaded (stress-free) states, which biases biomechanical simulations and inverse material identification. Existing approaches rarely recover the unloaded geometry and constitutive parameters jointly.
AI.method: A gradient-based inverse finite element framework that is fully differentiable and uses exact end-to-end gradients to simultaneously optimize geometry and constitutive parameters. The objective combines a nodal-position misfit with a deformation-gradient-based mismatch term to improve robustness under large deformations. Inputs are two or more observed deformed configurations.
AI.result: Benchmark studies quantify the influence of loading diversity and observation count and show reduced sensitivity to poor material initialization. Application to an MRI-derived breast model accurately recovers the unloaded configuration and constitutive parameters from multiple gravity-loaded states.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a unified and scalable tool for inverse biomechanics, with potential applications in personalized modeling, elastography, and surgical planning.

title: Microscopic theory of spin-torque ferromagnetic resonance in nonmagnetic-metal/ferromagnetic-metal heterostructures
summary: We develop a microscopic theory of spin-torque ferromagnetic resonance (ST-FMR) in nonmagnetic-metal/ferromagnetic-metal heterostructures. Tracing out the conduction-electron degrees of freedom in the FM, we derive an effective interfacial exchange coupling between the localized spins and the conduction electron spins in the adjacent electron system. Based on this interaction, we calculate the current-induced driving torque, resonance-frequency shift, damping modulation, and resulting dc voltage. As a concrete example, we apply the formulation to a disordered Rashba two-dimensional electron gas and demonstrate that the ST-FMR spectrum reflects the dynamical spin responses of the adjacent electron system. Our formulation applies to a broad class of heterostructures and establishes a unified microscopic framework connecting ST-FMR spectra directly to the electronic spin responses of adjacent systems.

AI.tldr: A microscopic theory of spin-torque ferromagnetic resonance (ST-FMR) in nonmagnetic-metal/ferromagnetic-metal heterostructures, showing that ST-FMR spectra directly reflect the dynamical spin responses of the adjacent electron system.
AI.motivation: Existing understanding of ST-FMR lacks a unified microscopic framework that directly links measured spectra to the electronic spin responses of the adjacent nonmagnetic system, which is needed to interpret experiments across diverse heterostructures.
AI.method: Trace out the conduction-electron degrees of freedom in the ferromagnet to derive an effective interfacial exchange coupling between localized spins and conduction electron spins in the adjacent electron system; use this interaction to calculate the current-induced driving torque, resonance-frequency shift, damping modulation, and resulting dc voltage; apply the formulation to a disordered Rashba two-dimensional electron gas.
AI.result: The ST-FMR spectrum is shown to reflect the dynamical spin responses of the adjacent electron system, as demonstrated through the disordered Rashba 2DEG example.
AI.conclusion: The formulation applies to a broad class of heterostructures and establishes a unified microscopic framework connecting ST-FMR spectra directly to the electronic spin responses of adjacent systems.

title: Atomic-scale structure of static screening in noble-metal nanoparticles from clusters to the conductor limit
summary: The static screening response of a metallic nanoparticle is encoded in its induced charge density. Integrated observables such as the dipole moment or the polarizability do not determine this density, because many different screening profiles yield the same integrals. We show that in noble-metal nanoparticles the screening charge is atomically structured, with facet, edge, and vertex sites responding differently from a smooth classical conductor. This structure survives in a surface layer of about one atomic width even when the integrated response has reached the conductor limit, and it is absent from continuum descriptions. To resolve it across size, morphology, and composition, we calibrate an atomistic charge-dipole model for Ag and Au nanoparticles directly to first-principles induced-density profiles. The calibration includes the short-range kinetic and exchange-correlation contribution to the hardness kernel that a purely electrostatic model omits, reducing the induced-density-profile error by about a factor of 2.5. A single averaged parameter set per element predicts clusters withheld from the fit and transfers without adjustment to Ag/Au core-shell, alloyed, and elongated particles. A continuous fast multipole implementation of the model scales almost linearly with the number of atoms and reaches several-million-atom particles, far beyond the reach of first-principles methods.

AI.tldr: Induced screening charge in noble-metal nanoparticles is atomically structured (facet, edge, vertex sites differ), persists in a ~one-atom-wide surface layer even at the conductor limit, and is captured by a calibrated atomistic charge-dipole model that scales to millions of atoms.
AI.motivation: Integrated observables like dipole moment and polarizability cannot uniquely determine the induced charge density, since many screening profiles yield identical integrals. Continuum/classical conductor descriptions miss the atomistic structure of the screening response, so a model resolving this structure across size, morphology, and composition is needed.
AI.method: The authors calibrate an atomistic charge-dipole model for Ag and Au nanoparticles directly against first-principles induced-density profiles. The calibration incorporates the short-range kinetic and exchange-correlation contribution to the hardness kernel omitted by purely electrostatic models. A continuous fast multipole implementation is used to scale the model.
AI.result: Screening charge is atomically structured, with facet, edge, and vertex sites responding differently from a smooth classical conductor; this structure survives in a surface layer of about one atomic width even when the integrated response reaches the conductor limit. Including the short-range kernel term reduces the induced-density-profile error by about a factor of 2.5. A single averaged parameter set per element predicts withheld clusters and transfers without adjustment to Ag/Au core-shell, alloyed, and elongated particles. The fast multipole implementation scales almost linearly with atom number, reaching several-million-atom particles.
AI.conclusion: Atomistic screening structure in noble-metal nanoparticles is real, resolvable, and modelable: a first-principles-calibrated charge-dipole model with short-range kernel corrections accurately reproduces induced-density profiles, generalizes across compositions and morphologies, and via fast multipole methods extends to particles far beyond the reach of first-principles calculations.

title: Electronic correlations shape the low-energy optical response of the kagome antiferromagnets Mn$_3$Sn and Mn$_3$Ge
summary: Using optical spectroscopy and density functional theory, we provide evidence that electron-electron interactions strongly affect the properties of the kagome antiferromagnet Mn$_3$Sn, since its low-energy optical interband transitions arise exclusively from the correlation-modified electronic band structure. Mn$_3$Sn possesses an optical effective mass about three times larger than that of its isostructural analog Mn$_3$Ge. The DFT+$U$ treatment in the Lichtenstein formulation, with an on-site Coulomb repulsion $U = 4$~eV and Hund's coupling $J = 0.25$~eV, accounts for the optical transitions in Mn$_3$Sn, whereas those in Mn$_3$Ge are already reproduced without Hubbard corrections ($U, J = 0$). The near-isotropic electronic structure of Mn$_3$Sn reveals a three-dimensional metal whose electronic response is shaped prominently by the Mn $d$-states. The apparent linear regime in $σ_1(ω)$ observed in Mn$_3$Sn and Mn$_3$Ge arises from several overlapping interband transitions and therefore should not be interpreted as the optical signature of the Weyl cones. The optical response does not alter with magnetic field up to 17 T, consistent with strong free-carrier screening. Our findings establish a comprehensive-correlated picture of Mn$_3$Sn and Mn$_3$Ge that offers a template for other correlated topological metals.

AI.tldr: Optical spectroscopy combined with DFT+$U$ shows that electron correlations, not topology, dominate the low-energy interband optical response of the kagome antiferromagnet Mn$_3$Sn, which has an optical effective mass roughly three times that of Mn$_3$Ge.
AI.motivation: Mn$_3$Sn is a kagome antiferromagnet often discussed as a topological (Weyl) metal, but the role of electron-electron interactions in shaping its electronic and optical properties was unclear. The authors aim to disentangle correlation effects from topological band features and to contrast Mn$_3$Sn with its isostructural analog Mn$_3$Ge.
AI.method: Optical spectroscopy (including $σ_1(ω)$) is used to extract low-energy interband transitions and the optical effective mass, complemented by density functional theory with Hubbard corrections. DFT+$U$ in the Lichtenstein formulation ($U = 4$ eV, $J = 0.25$ eV) is applied to Mn$_3$Sn, while Mn$_3$Ge is treated without Hubbard corrections ($U, J = 0$). Magneto-optical measurements extend to 17 T.
AI.result: The low-energy interband transitions in Mn$_3$Sn arise exclusively from a correlation-modified band structure, giving an optical effective mass about three times larger than Mn$_3$Ge. DFT+$U$ reproduces the optical transitions in Mn$_3$Sn, whereas Mn$_3$Ge is already described with $U, J = 0$. The electronic structure is near-isotropic and three-dimensional, shaped prominently by Mn $d$-states. The apparent linear regime in $σ_1(ω)$ stems from overlapping interband transitions rather than a Weyl-cone signature. The optical response is unchanged up to 17 T, consistent with strong free-carrier screening.
AI.conclusion: Mn$_3$Sn and Mn$_3$Ge are best described as strongly correlated topological metals whose optical response is governed by correlation-renormalized bands; the linear $σ_1(ω)$ should not be taken as evidence of Weyl cones. This correlated picture provides a template for other correlated topological metals.

title: Adaptive Substrate Support Based on Thin-Film Piezoelectric Actuators
summary: Advanced lithography scanners require extreme substrate flatness in the range of nanometers to prevent focus errors. Such a flatness is challenging to reach and maintain using static substrate supports. Active correction concepts using bulk piezoelectric or linear actuators become prohibitive due to wiring and volume limitations, considering the thousands of pillars required. In this work, we present to our knowledge the first ever demonstration of an active substrate support concept based on thin-film piezoelectric actuators. The working principle, fabrication steps, and characterization of a proof-of-principle device, supported by finite element modeling (FEM), are presented in detail. The fabricated device shows a displacement above 9 nm, which is sufficient to correct some of the focus errors in lithography systems. We foresee that this new concept may open the way towards smaller chip dimensions and improved yield.

AI.tldr: First demonstration of an active substrate support concept for lithography scanners using thin-film piezoelectric actuators, achieving >9 nm displacement sufficient to correct focus errors.
AI.motivation: Advanced lithography scanners require nanometer-range substrate flatness to prevent focus errors, but static supports cannot reach or maintain this. Bulk piezoelectric or linear actuator-based active correction is limited by wiring and volume constraints given the thousands of pillars needed.
AI.method: Proposes and demonstrates an active substrate support based on thin-film piezoelectric actuators. Details the working principle, fabrication steps, and characterization of a proof-of-principle device, supported by finite element modeling (FEM).
AI.result: The fabricated device achieves a displacement above 9 nm, sufficient to correct some focus errors in lithography systems.
AI.conclusion: This new thin-film piezoelectric active substrate support concept may enable smaller chip dimensions and improved yield.

title: Quantum electrodynamics of equilibrium systems: A rigorous Maxwell-regularized functional-theoretic formulation
summary: A framework for quantum electrodynamics of equilibrium systems is proposed that takes the Maxwell equations as foundational and links them to the structure of density-functional theory for the quantum system. By switching from purely internal observables like the one-particle density to combined internal and external quantities, the external sources and their energy are taken into account. A fully regularized functional theory emerges that avoids the usual representability problems. With the Kohn-Sham construction that links to an auxiliary uncoupled system, the ultra-violet cutoff can be removed and one arrives at a fully renormalized and non-perturbative light-matter description. Regularized forms of density-functional theory with and without magnetic fields appear as boundary cases, while the emergent physical picture reproduces the macroscopic Maxwell equations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a QED framework for equilibrium systems that grounds density-functional theory in Maxwell's equations by combining internal and external observables, yielding a fully regularized, renormalized, non-perturbative light-matter description.
AI.motivation: Conventional density-functional theory relies on internal observables (e.g., the one-particle density) and suffers from representability problems, and it does not natively accommodate the external electromagnetic sources and their energy. A formulation linking Maxwell's equations to the quantum system's density-functional structure is needed.
AI.method: The framework takes Maxwell's equations as foundational and switches from purely internal observables to combined internal-external quantities, incorporating external sources and their energy. A fully regularized functional theory is constructed, and a Kohn-Sham construction links the interacting system to an auxiliary uncoupled system, allowing the ultra-violet cutoff to be removed.
AI.result: A fully regularized functional theory is obtained that avoids usual representability problems. Removing the ultra-violet cutoff via the Kohn-Sham construction yields a fully renormalized, non-perturbative light-matter description. Regularized density-functional theories with and without magnetic fields emerge as boundary cases, and the physical picture reproduces the macroscopic Maxwell equations.
AI.conclusion: Grounding density-functional theory in Maxwell's equations via combined internal-external observables provides a regularized, renormalized, non-perturbative QED description of equilibrium light-matter systems that recovers known density-functional limits and macroscopic Maxwell behavior.

title: Van der Waals interactions in supercritical water under Earth's mantle conditions
summary: The properties of water under high pressure and high temperature (HP-HT) are critical in multiple geochemical processes in deep Earth. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) is a promising approach to study water under extreme conditions without any empirical parameters. However, the accuracy of AIMD simulations is determined by the exchange-correlation (XC) functional including the dispersion correction used in density functional theory calculations. While van der Waals (vdW) interactions are well known to be critically important for water under ambient conditions, the influence of the dispersion correction on the properties of HP-HT water as found in Earth's mantle remains largely unexplored. To address this, we carried out AIMD simulations for supercritical water at 1, 5, and 10 GPa, and 1000 K. We compared PBE, PBE-D3, RPBE-D3, and SCAN functionals, where D3 means Grimme's D3 dispersion correction. We compared the structural, diffusion, and vibrational properties of water as computed with these XC functionals. Overall, the discrepancies between the functionals are reduced under extreme P-T conditions relative to ambient conditions. PBE and PBE-D3 exhibit higher proton-transfer rates than RPBE-D3 and SCAN, suggesting that while vdW interactions do not significantly affect the water structure under extreme conditions, the oxygen-hydrogen bond strength does influence proton transfer. Our results provide molecular-level insight into water in Earth's mantle and offer valuable guidance for selecting appropriate XC functionals in AIMD simulations of aqueous solutions under extreme conditions.

AI.tldr: This study uses AIMD simulations to assess how the exchange-correlation (XC) functional and dispersion correction affect the properties of supercritical water at 1, 5, and 10 GPa and 1000 K, finding that functional discrepancies shrink under extreme P-T conditions and that O-H bond strength, more than vdW interactions, governs proton transfer.
AI.motivation: Water's properties under high-pressure, high-temperature (HP-HT) conditions are critical for geochemical processes in deep Earth, and AIMD offers a parameter-free route to study them. However, AIMD accuracy depends on the XC functional and its dispersion correction. While vdW interactions are known to matter for ambient water, their influence on HP-HT water relevant to Earth's mantle is largely unexplored.
AI.method: AIMD simulations of supercritical water at 1, 5, and 10 GPa and 1000 K were performed. Four functionals were compared: PBE, PBE-D3, RPBE-D3, and SCAN, where D3 denotes Grimme's D3 dispersion correction. Structural, diffusion, and vibrational properties were computed and compared across these XC functionals.
AI.result: Discrepancies between functionals are reduced under extreme P-T conditions compared to ambient conditions. PBE and PBE-D3 show higher proton-transfer rates than RPBE-D3 and SCAN. This indicates that vdW interactions do not significantly affect water structure under extreme conditions, whereas the oxygen-hydrogen bond strength does influence proton transfer.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide molecular-level insight into water in Earth's mantle and offer practical guidance for selecting appropriate XC functionals in AIMD simulations of aqueous solutions under extreme conditions.

title: Landscape geometry of Majorana zero modes in inhomogeneous superconductors
summary: Spatial inhomogeneity breaks translational symmetry and prevents conventional Bloch-band topological invariants from directly answering a practical question: do Majorana zero modes survive in a given inhomogeneous superconducting device? In this Letter, we develop a real-space landscape approach to address this question. Rather than solving the zero-energy equation as a boundary-value problem, we treat the spatial coordinate as an evolution parameter and recast the equation as a first-order dynamical system. A Majorana zero mode is then identified with a stable trajectory that satisfies the physical boundary condition and approaches the origin at large distance. We show that the landscape geometry fixes the dimensions of the stable and unstable subspaces, while the intersection of the stable subspace with the physical boundary subspace determines the number of Majorana zero modes. In the homogeneous limit, the topological phase transition is manifested as a geometric transition of the landscape. Applied to one-dimensional spinless $p$-wave superconductors and nanowire--superconductor systems, the approach yields sufficient bounds on both the amplitude and spatial gradient of the inhomogeneity, providing quantitative criteria for the design of Majorana devices.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce a real-space landscape approach to determine whether Majorana zero modes survive in inhomogeneous superconducting devices, reformulating the zero-energy equation as a dynamical system where MZMs correspond to stable trajectories reaching the origin. The landscape geometry governs stable/unstable subspace dimensions, and the intersection of the stable subspace with the physical boundary subspace yields the MZM count. Applied to 1D spinless p-wave superconductors and nanowire-superconductor systems, it provides sufficient bounds on inhomogeneity amplitude and spatial gradient.
AI.motivation: Spatial inhomogeneity breaks translational symmetry, so conventional Bloch-band topological invariants cannot directly answer whether Majorana zero modes survive in a given inhomogeneous superconducting device. A method that works directly in real space is needed.
AI.method: Instead of solving the zero-energy equation as a boundary-value problem, the spatial coordinate is treated as an evolution parameter and the equation is recast as a first-order dynamical system. A Majorana zero mode is identified with a stable trajectory satisfying the physical boundary condition and approaching the origin at large distance. The landscape geometry fixes the dimensions of stable and unstable subspaces, and the intersection of the stable subspace with the physical boundary subspace determines the number of Majorana zero modes.
AI.result: In the homogeneous limit, the topological phase transition manifests as a geometric transition of the landscape. For 1D spinless p-wave superconductors and nanowire-superconductor systems, the approach yields sufficient bounds on both the amplitude and spatial gradient of the inhomogeneity.
AI.conclusion: The real-space landscape approach provides quantitative criteria for the design of Majorana devices, enabling assessment of MZM survival under inhomogeneity without relying on translational symmetry.

title: The quantum Mpemba effect in symmetric random Clifford circuits
summary: The quantum Mpemba effect is the counterintuitive phenomenon whereby a quantum state initially farther from equilibrium relaxes faster than one initially closer to it. We demonstrate this effect in random Clifford circuits with a conserved $\mathrm{U}(1)$ charge, using the entanglement asymmetry to characterize relaxation through dynamical symmetry restoration. Exact numerical simulations show that an initially more asymmetric state can become locally more symmetric than an initially less asymmetric one. We explain this behavior by mapping the dynamics onto a charge-conserving quantum automaton, in which the decay of the entanglement asymmetry is controlled by the statistics of encounters between two particle species evolving according to a symmetric simple exclusion process. This mapping yields an analytic expression for the entanglement asymmetry and provides a simple microscopic mechanism for the quantum Mpemba effect: stronger initial symmetry breaking corresponds to a denser particle configuration, which enhances the frequency of particle encounters and thereby accelerates symmetry restoration.

AI.tldr: The quantum Mpemba effect is demonstrated in random Clifford circuits with a conserved U(1) charge, where a more asymmetric initial state relaxes faster via dynamical symmetry restoration, explained through a mapping to a charge-conserving quantum automaton.
AI.motivation: The quantum Mpemba effect—where a state farther from equilibrium relaxes faster than one closer to it—is counterintuitive and lacks a clear microscopic understanding in the context of symmetry restoration dynamics.
AI.method: Exact numerical simulations of random Clifford circuits with conserved U(1) charge, using the entanglement asymmetry as the relaxation metric; mapping the dynamics onto a charge-conserving quantum automaton governed by encounters between two particle species obeying a symmetric simple exclusion process.
AI.result: An initially more asymmetric state can become locally more symmetric than an initially less asymmetric one; the mapping yields an analytic expression for the entanglement asymmetry.
AI.conclusion: The quantum Mpemba effect arises because stronger initial symmetry breaking corresponds to a denser particle configuration, increasing encounter frequency and thus accelerating symmetry restoration.

title: Exact and fast series expansions for quantum models with long-range interactions
summary: Over the past decade, high-order series expansions based on linked-cluster methods have become an important tool for studying low-energy properties of gapped quantum systems with long-range interactions. We introduce a deterministic framework that removes a central computational bottleneck of this method. Our graph zeta method replaces the costly and statistically noisy Monte Carlo (MC) evaluation of high-dimensional lattice sums by a systematic, high-precision computation that delivers series coefficients within minutes on standard desktop hardware. The full momentum-dependent series is obtained in a single calculation, enabling high-resolution excitation spectra throughout the Brillouin zone. Building on the companion paper [1], the method reformulates graph-embedding sums as graph zeta functions and decomposes them into blocks classified by their treewidth tw. Low-treewidth blocks (tw$\leq2$) admit closed expressions based on Epstein zeta functions, while higher-treewidth blocks (tw$>2$) are evaluated using tensor-network bucket elimination. We benchmark the approach for transverse-field Ising models with power-law interactions in 1d, 2d, and 3d, reproducing previous MC results at a fraction of the computational cost while enabling substantially denser parameter sampling. An open-source implementation makes the method directly applicable to general interactions and large parameter scans. As an application, we compare microscopic interaction models for the stacked quasi-2d transverse-field Ising triangular-lattice antiferromagnet KTmSe$_2$ and find that a model including dipolar interactions best describes existing experimental data. The graph zeta method thus turns high-order linked-cluster expansions into a practical and deterministic tool for fast quantitative momentum-resolved modeling of short- and long-range quantum matter.

AI.tldr: A deterministic graph zeta method replaces Monte Carlo evaluation of lattice sums in high-order linked-cluster expansions, enabling fast, high-precision, momentum-resolved series for gapped quantum systems with long-range interactions.
AI.motivation: High-order series expansions via linked-cluster methods are key for low-energy properties of gapped quantum systems with long-range interactions, but they suffer from a central computational bottleneck: the costly and statistically noisy Monte Carlo evaluation of high-dimensional lattice sums.
AI.method: The method reformulates graph-embedding sums as graph zeta functions, decomposing them into blocks classified by treewidth tw. Low-treewidth blocks (tw≤2) get closed expressions via Epstein zeta functions; higher-treewidth blocks (tw>2) are evaluated using tensor-network bucket elimination. The full momentum-dependent series is obtained in a single calculation.
AI.result: Benchmarked on transverse-field Ising models with power-law interactions in 1d, 2d, and 3d, the approach reproduces previous MC results at a fraction of the computational cost, delivers series coefficients within minutes on standard desktop hardware, and enables denser parameter sampling and high-resolution excitation spectra across the Brillouin zone. For KTmSe2, a dipolar-interaction model best fits experimental data.
AI.conclusion: The graph zeta method turns high-order linked-cluster expansions into a practical, deterministic, open-source tool for fast quantitative momentum-resolved modeling of short- and long-range quantum matter.

title: Epitaxial inversion of spontaneous polarization in ε-Ga2O3
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures in manuscript, 3 figures in SI
summary: Polar wide bandgap semiconductors offer the unique capability to manipulate internal electric fields and induce two-dimensional electron gases (2DEG). The emerging orthorhombic ε-Ga2O3 is a promising candidate owing to its large spontaneous polarization (Psp). However, exploiting this material is hindered by fundamental ambiguities surrounding its absolute Psp vectors and the inability to govern its epitaxial direction. Here we show the resolution of the absolute Psp vectors in ε-Ga2O3 and control of its macroscopic polarity via substrate engineering. By correlating interferometric piezoresponse with atomic configurations, we establish an identification criterion where opposing polarities are assigned through the geometric elevation within an asymmetric four-atom sequence. Guided by this signature, we demonstrate that epitaxy on Al-polar AlN and sapphire yields uniformly Ga-polar (upward Psp) and O-polar (downward Psp) architectures, respectively, whereas deteriorated crystallinity disrupts this registry and triggers mixed-polarity. This atomic-to-macroscopic correlation eliminates long-standing ambiguities regarding absolute polar orientations in non-centrosymmetric oxides. Analogous to mature III-Nitride architectures, this blueprint provides the foundational platform for designing macroscopic polarization discontinuities at heterointerfaces, unlocking ε-Ga2O3 for advanced polarization electronics.

AI.tldr: This work resolves the absolute spontaneous polarization (Psp) vectors of orthorhombic ε-Ga2O3 and demonstrates substrate-controlled macroscopic polarity, establishing a foundation for polarization electronics based on this polar wide bandgap oxide.
AI.motivation: Polar wide bandgap semiconductors can manipulate internal electric fields and induce 2DEGs. ε-Ga2O3 is a promising candidate due to its large spontaneous polarization, but its exploitation is hindered by ambiguities in its absolute Psp vectors and the inability to control its epitaxial polarity.

They then perform substrate engineering, growing ε-Ga2O3 on Al-polar AlN and sapphire to control macroscopic polarity.
