title: Direct observation of phonon mode with an antisymmetric Raman tensor
summary: Phonon angular momentum, characterized by circular or elliptical motion of atoms, plays a decisive role in diverse phenomena, ranging from the phonon Hall effect, phonon magnetic moment, Einstein-de Haas effect, Weyl phonons, and driven chiral phonons. The phonon modes with an antisymmetric Raman tensor, which carry an intrinsic phonon angular momentum in a pseudovector symmetry channel, have been overlooked in the past in the chiral phonon community. Here, we report the detection of this type of phonon mode using polarization-resolved Raman spectroscopy. We observe a phonon at 266cm$^{-1}$ in the antiferromagnetic chiral phase of Cr$_2$O$_3$ in the $A_2$-pseudovector symmetry channel. This $A_2$ mode's frequency and the elliptical motion are captured by first-principles phonon calculations, which treat both lattice and spins on an equal footing as 'slow' degrees of freedom. This mode gets Raman activity due to the presence of Cr vacancies in Cr$_2$O$_3$ that locally break the twofold rotational symmetry perpendicular to the threefold axis. Our results provide a new way to detect the novel symmetry-forbidden $A_2$ phonon modes with an antisymmetric Raman tensor in a pseudovector symmetry channel.

AI.motivation: Phonon angular momentum—arising from circular or elliptical atomic motion—governs phenomena such as the phonon Hall effect, phonon magnetic moment, Einstein–de Haas effect, Weyl phonons, and driven chiral phonons. However, phonon modes with an antisymmetric Raman tensor that carry intrinsic phonon angular momentum in a pseudovector symmetry channel have been overlooked within the chiral phonon community.
AI.method: Polarization-resolved Raman spectroscopy is applied to the antiferromagnetic chiral phase of Cr₂O₃. First-principles phonon calculations treat lattice and spins on an equal footing as 'slow' degrees of freedom to capture the A₂ mode's frequency and elliptical motion.
AI.result: A phonon at 266 cm⁻¹ is observed in the A₂-pseudovector symmetry channel. Its frequency and elliptical motion are reproduced by first-principles calculations. The mode acquires Raman activity because Cr vacancies locally break the twofold rotational symmetry perpendicular to the threefold axis.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a new route to detect novel symmetry-forbidden A₂ phonon modes possessing an antisymmetric Raman tensor in a pseudovector symmetry channel.

title: Moment-informed force rescaling for random-batch Langevin dynamics
summary: Random-batch methods accelerate molecular dynamics by replacing full interaction sums with stochastic force estimators. In Langevin simulations, however, random-batch force errors can cause artificial heating and distort equilibrium and dynamical observables, especially for small batch sizes or under weak thermostat coupling. Moreover, the magnitude of these errors can vary across particles. We introduce moment-informed force rescaling for random-batch list (Mi-RBL) and random-batch Ewald (Mi-RBE) methods. A lagged average of each particle's sampled-force intensity sets an isotropic gain before the current batch is sampled, changing the random-batch force magnitude without changing its direction. The formal finite-time analysis quantifies the bias--variance tradeoff, and an estimate of the steady-state kinetic-temperature error predicts the scaling of the kinetic error with time step and thermostat friction. In the coexistence, binary-mixture, and electrolyte tests, Mi-RBL and Mi-RBE reduce kinetic errors and more closely reproduce the mean-square displacement, radial distribution function, and charge density profiles of the reference solutions. Mi-RBE also reduces the growth rate of the kinetic error with the time step by more than half and retains the predicted dependence on thermostat friction. The tested rescaling strength decreases with increasing batch size, and the particlewise update retains $O(N)$ complexity for fixed batch size.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces moment-informed force rescaling (Mi-RBL, Mi-RBE) that isotropically scales random-batch forces using a lagged average of each particle's sampled-force intensity, reducing artificial heating and kinetic-temperature errors in Langevin molecular dynamics while preserving O(N) complexity.
AI.motivation: Random-batch methods accelerate molecular dynamics by substituting full interaction sums with stochastic force estimators, but in Langevin simulations the resulting force errors cause artificial heating and distort equilibrium and dynamical observables. This is especially problematic at small batch sizes or weak thermostat coupling, and error magnitudes vary across particles, motivating a correction that improves accuracy without sacrificing efficiency.
AI.method: The authors propose moment-informed force rescaling for random-batch list (Mi-RBL) and random-batch Ewald (Mi-RBE). A lagged average of each particle's sampled-force intensity sets an isotropic gain applied before the current batch is sampled, altering the random-batch force magnitude but not its direction. A formal finite-time analysis quantifies the bias--variance tradeoff, and a steady-state kinetic-temperature error estimate predicts the scaling of kinetic error with time step and thermostat friction.
AI.result: In coexistence, binary-mixture, and electrolyte tests, Mi-RBL and Mi-RBE reduce kinetic errors and more closely reproduce reference mean-square displacement, radial distribution function, and charge density profiles. Mi-RBE cuts the growth rate of kinetic error with time step by more than half and retains the predicted dependence on thermostat friction. The tested rescaling strength decreases with increasing batch size, and the particlewise update preserves O(N) complexity for fixed batch size.
AI.conclusion: Moment-informed isotropic force rescaling is an effective, low-cost remedy for random-batch force-error-induced heating and observable distortion in Langevin molecular dynamics, with theoretical bias--variance characterization and scaling predictions validated by numerical tests across multiple systems.

title: Tuneable terahertz transitions in zigzag graphene nanoribbons
summary: We show that a transverse electric field applied to a zigzag graphene nanoribbon opens a band gap whose energy can be tuned through the terahertz (THz) range. The field breaks the reflection symmetry of the ribbon, allowing optical transitions that are forbidden in its absence. The relative strengths of transitions polarized parallel and transverse to the ribbon depend strongly on excitation frequency and become equal at a particular frequency. At this frequency, each helicity selectively excites carriers in only one of the two field-induced edge-state valleys, with the selected valley reversed for the opposite helicity. Since this excitation occurs away from the valley minima, the photoexcited carriers have finite group velocity, giving rise to a circular photogalvanic response. Van Hove singularities enhance radiative recombination at the band edge, providing a route towards compact, tunable THz emitters.

AI.tldr: A transverse electric field opens a tunable THz band gap in zigzag graphene nanoribbons and enables helicity-dependent valley-selective optical excitation, yielding a circular photogalvanic response and potential THz emitters.
AI.motivation: Graphene lacks an intrinsic band gap, limiting its use in optoelectronic devices. The paper aims to show how a transverse electric field in zigzag graphene nanoribbons can break reflection symmetry, create a tunable THz gap, and enable novel valley-selective optical and photogalvanic functionalities.
AI.method: The authors analyze the electronic and optical response of zigzag graphene nanoribbons under a transverse electric field. They examine symmetry breaking, optical transition selection rules, polarization-dependent transition strengths, helicity-resolved valley excitation, carrier group velocities, circular photogalvanic response, and Van Hove singularities at the band edge.
AI.result: The transverse field opens a band gap tunable through the THz range, activates otherwise forbidden optical transitions, and makes parallel- and transverse-polarized transition strengths equal at a specific frequency. At that frequency, each helicity selectively excites carriers in one field-induced edge-state valley, with the opposite helicity reversing the selected valley. Because excitation occurs away from the valley minima, photoexcited carriers have finite group velocity, producing a circular photogalvanic response. Van Hove singularities enhance radiative recombination at the band edge.
AI.conclusion: A transverse electric field in zigzag graphene nanoribbons provides a route to tunable THz band gaps, helicity-controlled valley-selective carrier excitation, and a circular photogalvanic response. The enhanced band-edge radiative recombination suggests potential for compact, tunable THz emitters.

title: Entropy Estimates from Stochastic Interpolants
summary: We present a general method for estimating entropy differences between arbitrary probability distributions using stochastic interpolants. The marginal distributions which bridge the base and target obey a continuity equation, which allows a straightforward calculation of the entropy difference in terms of an inner product of the probability flow velocity and score fields. This formulation has several advantages: (i) no computationally expensive divergence calculations of either field are required, (ii) the score field need not even be learned directly if model transferability is not required, and (iii) on-the-fly estimates are produced nearly for free during training. When tractable base distributions are chosen (e.g. Gaussian chain, ideal gas, etc.), statistical thermodynamic entropies are then immediately recovered. Notably, the analysis relies only on the definition of the Gibbs-Shannon entropy, rather than any particular statistical mechanical ensemble, so that generalized non-equilibrium entropies may be computed. The method is demonstrated on several systems of increasing complexity: (i) a 40-dimensional Gaussian mixture model, (ii) the classical XY model of N spins arranged in one dimension, (iii) the 13-atom Lennard-Jones cluster, and (iv) an active Brownian polymer.

AI.tldr: A general method estimates entropy differences between arbitrary distributions via stochastic interpolants, computing entropy as an inner product of probability flow velocity and score fields without expensive divergence calculations, with on-the-fly estimates during training.
AI.motivation: Computing entropy differences between probability distributions typically requires expensive divergence calculations or direct learning of score fields. The authors seek a general, cheap, and flexible formulation that relies only on the Gibbs-Shannon entropy definition, enabling both statistical thermodynamic entropies and generalized non-equilibrium entropies.
AI.method: Using stochastic interpolants, the marginal distributions bridging a base and target distribution obey a continuity equation. This allows the entropy difference to be expressed as an inner product of the probability flow velocity and score fields, avoiding divergence computations and allowing the score field to remain implicit when model transferability is not needed.
AI.result: On-the-fly estimates are produced nearly for free during training. With tractable base distributions (e.g. Gaussian chain, ideal gas), statistical thermodynamic entropies are immediately recovered. The method is validated on four systems of increasing complexity: a 40-dimensional Gaussian mixture model, the classical 1D XY model of N spins, the 13-atom Lennard-Jones cluster, and an active Brownian polymer.
AI.conclusion: The proposed stochastic-interpolant formulation provides a practical, general estimator of entropy differences that avoids costly divergence terms and is broadly applicable, from standard statistical mechanical ensembles to generalized non-equilibrium entropies.

title: Floquet-Plasmon Enhanced Charge Transfer at Catalytic Interfaces
summary: Plasmonic excitation of metallic nanostructures can generate energetic carriers capable of transferring charge into nearby adsorbed molecules, providing a possible pathway for driving chemical transformations. In many theoretical descriptions of this process, charge transfer is determined by the equilibrium electronic structure of the molecule and substrate together with the time-dependent carrier distribution produced during plasmon decay. However, the intense transient electric fields associated with localized surface plasmons can also dynamically perturb the molecular electronic structure itself on ultrafast timescales. In this work, we investigate how these time-dependent fields modify the molecular spectral function and influence charge injection at catalytic interfaces. Using a model of CO2 adsorbed on Au(111), we compute the real-time molecular Green's function within a correlated frontier-orbital active space under plasmon-like driving. We find that the driving field rapidly produces transient Floquet-type replica bands in the molecular density of states, opening additional resonant pathways for hot-carrier injection that are absent without external driving or in time-local descriptions. Coupling the evolving molecular spectrum to a time-dependent hot-electron distribution described within a two-temperature Sommerfeld framework, we predict large enhancements in quasiparticle spectral overlap that governs injection during plasmon dephasing. These results suggest that dynamically generated non-equilibrium spectral structure may play an important role in plasmon-assisted catalysis and provide a framework for studying driven catalytic interfaces beyond static electronic structure descriptions.

AI.tldr: This work shows that intense transient plasmonic fields dynamically modify the molecular spectral function of CO2 on Au(111), producing transient Floquet-type replica bands that open extra resonant hot-carrier injection pathways, dramatically enhancing spectral overlap and injection during plasmon dephasing beyond static descriptions.
AI.motivation: Standard theoretical treatments of plasmon-driven charge transfer rely on the equilibrium electronic structure of molecule plus substrate combined with a time-dependent carrier distribution from plasmon decay. However, intense transient fields of localized surface plasmons can themselves dynamically perturb molecular electronic structure on ultrafast timescales, an effect largely neglected. This paper aims to capture how such time-dependent fields reshape the molecular spectral function and alter charge injection at catalytic interfaces.
AI.method: Using a model of CO2 adsorbed on Au(111), the authors compute the real-time molecular Green's function within a correlated frontier-orbital active space under plasmon-like driving. The evolving molecular spectrum is coupled to a time-dependent hot-electron distribution described within a two-temperature Sommerfeld framework, allowing evaluation of quasiparticle spectral overlap that governs injection during plasmon dephasing.
AI.result: The driving field rapidly generates transient Floquet-type replica bands in the molecular density of states, creating additional resonant pathways for hot-carrier injection that are absent without external driving or in time-local descriptions. Coupling the evolving spectrum to the two-temperature hot-electron distribution predicts large enhancements in quasiparticle spectral overlap governing injection during plasmon dephasing.
AI.conclusion: Dynamically generated non-equilibrium spectral structure may play an important role in plasmon-assisted catalysis. The framework enables study of driven catalytic interfaces beyond static electronic structure descriptions.

title: Spinon-Induced Phonon Dynamics in Chiral and $π$-Flux Quantum Spin Liquids
summary: Quantum spin liquids (QSLs) are magnetic phases that evade long-range order down to the lowest temperatures due to strong quantum fluctuations. Their lack of conventional order parameters, however, makes experimental identification challenging. In this work, we investigate how distinct QSL phases affect phonon dynamics through spinon-phonon coupling. By computing the phonon self-energy, we show that the phonon spectrum remains unrenormalized by spinon interactions, while sound attenuation and phonon thermal conductivity exhibit distinct signatures of the underlying QSL phase. These response functions therefore provide experimentally accessible fingerprints for distinguishing different QSL backgrounds. Remarkably, we find that a chiral QSL coupled to phonons does not generate a phonon thermal Hall effect despite explicitly breaking time-reversal symmetry. Our results establish phonon transport as a potential probe for identifying and characterizing quantum spin liquids.

Notably, a chiral QSL does not produce a phonon thermal Hall effect despite broken time-reversal symmetry.
AI.motivation: QSLs evade long-range magnetic order due to strong quantum fluctuations and thus lack conventional order parameters, making their experimental identification challenging. The paper seeks an experimentally accessible probe to distinguish distinct QSL phases.
AI.method: The authors investigate how distinct QSL phases affect phonon dynamics via spinon-phonon coupling, computing the phonon self-energy to derive phonon spectrum, sound attenuation, and phonon thermal conductivity responses, including the case of a chiral QSL with explicitly broken time-reversal symmetry.
AI.result: The phonon spectrum remains unrenormalized by spinon interactions, whereas sound attenuation and phonon thermal conductivity show distinct signatures of the underlying QSL phase. A chiral QSL coupled to phonons does not generate a phonon thermal Hall effect despite broken time-reversal symmetry.
AI.conclusion: Phonon transport constitutes a potential probe for identifying and characterizing quantum spin liquids, with sound attenuation and thermal conductivity serving as experimentally accessible fingerprints of different QSL backgrounds.

title: Complex magnetic properties of EuAgAs single crystals
summary: EuAgAs is an antiferromagnetic topological material exhibiting intriguing magnetic behavior. We investigate its structural, magnetic, and local electronic properties using X ray diffraction, Mössbauer spectroscopy, dc magnetization, ac susceptibility, and heat capacity measurements. The results confirm antiferromagnetic ordering below $T_\text{N}$ and reveal pronounced magnetic anisotropy and several field induced metamagnetic transitions. We construct the magnetic phase diagram of EuAgAs, identifying several distinct magnetic regions. The field and temperature dependent behavior observed suggests a noncollinear magnetic structure in the low field regime. The sequence of field induced transitions resembles that observed in centrosymmetric rare earth compounds hosting skyrmion phases, suggesting that competing magnetic interactions may play an important role in stabilizing the observed magnetic states.

AI.tldr: Structural, magnetic, and local electronic studies of EuAgAs confirm antiferromagnetic ordering below TN with strong anisotropy, field-induced metamagnetic transitions, and a multi-region magnetic phase diagram suggesting a noncollinear low-field structure.
AI.motivation: EuAgAs is an antiferromagnetic topological material with intriguing magnetic behavior, motivating a detailed characterization of its structural, magnetic, and local electronic properties.
AI.method: X-ray diffraction, Mössbauer spectroscopy, dc magnetization, ac susceptibility, and heat capacity measurements.
AI.result: Antiferromagnetic ordering below TN is confirmed. Pronounced magnetic anisotropy and several field-induced metamagnetic transitions are observed. A magnetic phase diagram with several distinct regions is constructed, and the field/temperature-dependent behavior indicates a noncollinear magnetic structure in the low-field regime.
AI.conclusion: The sequence of field-induced transitions resembles that of centrosymmetric rare-earth compounds hosting skyrmion phases, suggesting competing magnetic interactions play an important role in stabilizing the observed magnetic states.

title: Altermagnetic Magnons in Dipolar Nanomagnet Arrays
comment: main: 9 pages, 4 figures; supplement: 7 pages, 2 figures
summary: Altermagnetism is conventionally understood in a spin-conserving framework, where symmetry-enforced momentum-dependent spin splitting emerges in collinear magnets with vanishing net magnetization. Here, we show that its defining signatures persist in nanomagnet arrays coupled exclusively by dipolar interactions, despite the intrinsic breaking of spin conservation. Using a macrospin theory of dipolar-coupled ferromagnetic nanoislands, corroborated by micromagnetic simulations, we demonstrate that arrays engineered with altermagnetic symmetries exhibit spin-split magnon bands whose eigenstates can partially remain strongly spin polarized. The resulting spin expectation value displays the characteristic $d$-wave pattern throughout the Brillouin zone, establishing a mesoscopic realization of altermagnetic magnons beyond the conventional spin-conserving paradigm. As a consequence, spin-wave propagation becomes strongly direction dependent, providing a highly tunable platform for anisotropic magnon transport and synthetic altermagnetic functionality.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that altermagnetic signatures, specifically $d$-wave spin-split magnon bands, can emerge in dipolar-coupled nanomagnet arrays even without spin conservation, establishing a mesoscopic realization of altermagnetic magnons.
AI.motivation: Altermagnetism is traditionally defined within a spin-conserving framework requiring momentum-dependent spin splitting in collinear magnets with zero net magnetization. The authors aim to test whether these defining signatures survive when spin conservation is intrinsically broken, as in dipolar-coupled systems.
AI.method: The authors employ a macrospin theory of dipolar-coupled ferromagnetic nanoislands, corroborated by micromagnetic simulations, engineering arrays with altermagnetic symmetries.
AI.result: The engineered arrays exhibit spin-split magnon bands whose eigenstates can remain strongly spin polarized, with the spin expectation value displaying a characteristic $d$-wave pattern across the Brillouin zone. Spin-wave propagation becomes strongly direction dependent.
AI.conclusion: Altermagnetic magnons can be realized beyond the conventional spin-conserving paradigm in mesoscopic dipolar-coupled nanomagnet arrays, providing a tunable platform for anisotropic magnon transport and synthetic altermagnetic functionality.

title: Logarithmic singularity in a dynamical quantum phase transition for free fermions
summary: We study the Loschmidt echo in a system of N non-interacting spinless lattice fermions released from a double-domain-wall initial state. In the large-N limit, the return probability is characterized by a large-deviation rate function known as the dynamical free energy. The Loschmidt echo is dominated by a complex instanton configuration, and the dynamical free energy develops a logarithmic singularity at the dynamical quantum phase transition. We obtain analytical results in the short-time and long-time regimes and support them with numerical computations. We show that the transition can be understood as a topological change of the dominant instanton configuration, analogous to the emergence of a cut in random matrix theory. We further show that post-selection can drive the system through two successive DQPTs, associated with successive topological changes of the dominant instanton configuration in complex time.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the Loschmidt echo for N non-interacting spinless lattice fermions starting from a double-domain-wall state, deriving the dynamical free energy via a complex instanton configuration and showing that the dynamical quantum phase transition corresponds to a topological change of the dominant instanton.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to characterize the return probability and dynamical quantum phase transition (DQPT) in a fermionic lattice system evolving from a double-domain-wall initial state, using a large-deviation (dynamical free energy) framework.
AI.method: They take the large-N limit to describe the return probability through a large-deviation rate function (dynamical free energy), dominated by a complex instanton configuration. They derive analytical results in short- and long-time regimes and corroborate them numerically. They map the transition to a topological change of the dominant instanton, analogous to a cut emerging in random matrix theory, and additionally consider post-selection driving the system through successive DQPTs.

The transition is identified as a topological change of the dominant instanton configuration (analogous to a random-matrix cut). Post-selection can drive the system through two successive DQPTs, linked to successive topological changes of the dominant instanton in complex time.
AI.conclusion: The DQPT in this double-domain-wall fermionic system is governed by topological changes of the dominant complex instanton configuration, and post-selection enables multiple successive transitions, extending the instanton-based understanding of DQPTs.

title: Electronic Origins of Elastic Behavior in Rocksalt, Zinc-Blende and Wurtzite 3d Transition-Metal Nitrides
summary: We present a comprehensive ab-initio study of the elastic properties of the IV-period transition metal nitrides, highlighting the correlation between their mechanical behavior and electronic structure. By analyzing the electronic density of states, we reveal how the occupation of bonding or antibonding orbitals determines the evolution of elastic properties along the period. Furthermore, we examine trends across different crystal structures, specifically comparing rocksalt, zincblende and wurtzite phases, to uncover how variations in crystal symmetry and atomic coordination influence their elastic properties.

AI.tldr: This ab-initio study links the elastic properties of IV-period transition metal nitrides to their electronic structure, showing how bonding/antibonding orbital occupation and crystal structure (rocksalt, zincblende, wurtzite) govern mechanical trends.
AI.motivation: The elastic behavior of IV-period transition metal nitrides is not well understood mechanistically, particularly how electronic structure and crystal symmetry/atomic coordination determine mechanical trends. The paper aims to close this gap.
AI.method: Comprehensive ab-initio calculations of elastic properties for IV-period transition metal nitrides. Analysis of the electronic density of states to correlate bonding and antibonding orbital occupation with elastic property evolution. Comparative study across rocksalt, zincblende, and wurtzite crystal structures to assess effects of symmetry and coordination.
AI.result: Occupation of bonding versus antibonding orbitals is shown to govern the systematic evolution of elastic properties along the period. Differences in crystal symmetry and atomic coordination across rocksalt, zincblende, and wurtzite phases are found to modulate the elastic response.
AI.conclusion: Elastic properties of IV-period transition metal nitrides are fundamentally controlled by electronic structure—specifically bonding/antibonding orbital occupation—and further tuned by crystal structure, providing a predictive framework linking electronic and mechanical behavior.

title: Load balancing for adaptive-precision interatomic potentials in materials science
summary: For atomistic molecular dynamics simulations, we consider a recently developed hybrid coupling between the highly accurate machine learning (ML)-based atomic cluster expansion (ACE) interaction model and a less precise (but about 1-2 orders faster) EAM potential, in order to leverage the performance bottleneck of pure ML potentials in a parallel computing environment. This spatial-temporal adaptivity has the potential for a speedup of more than an order of magnitude, that would be lost without a dynamic load-balancing strategy that becomes critical due to fluctuating potential contributions. We compare the load-balancing strategies of LAMMPS with load-balancing methods provided by the library ALL in adaptive-precision EAM-ACE simulations of a copper nanoindentation. For a regular-grid domain decomposition, the modified tensor method of the ALL library, which conserves the simplicity and transferability of the tensor method, significantly reduces the imbalance factor of the force calculation from 3.0 to 1.7 compared to the native load-balancing method of LAMMPS. A nearly perfectly balanced system with an imbalance factor close to 1.0 can be reached by load balancing an irregular grid of domains with the recursive bisectioning method of LAMMPS and with ALL's histogram method for a staggered grid of domains. Load balancing a staggered grid with ALL is found to be significantly faster than load balancing an irregular grid with the bisectioning method of LAMMPS, but the communication costs during a regular timestep are lower for the irregular grid of domains, as a lower surface-by-volume ratio of the domains is reached. Furthermore, we suggest a strategy to find the ideal load-balancing frequency for adaptive-precision simulations.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates dynamic load-balancing strategies for adaptive-precision EAM-ACE molecular dynamics simulations of copper nanoindentation, comparing LAMMPS native methods with the ALL library's tensor, recursive bisectioning, and histogram approaches.
AI.motivation: Pure machine-learning potentials such as ACE are highly accurate but computationally expensive, forming a performance bottleneck in parallel simulations. A hybrid EAM-ACE coupling with spatial-temporal adaptivity can yield over an order-of-magnitude speedup, but this benefit is lost without dynamic load balancing, which becomes critical due to fluctuating potential contributions across the domain.
AI.method: The authors compare load-balancing strategies of LAMMPS against those provided by the ALL library within adaptive-precision EAM-ACE simulations of a copper nanoindentation system. They examine a regular-grid domain decomposition using ALL's modified tensor method and LAMMPS's native method, an irregular grid using LAMMPS's recursive bisectioning, and a staggered grid using ALL's histogram method, measuring imbalance factors and communication costs.
AI.result: For a regular-grid decomposition, ALL's modified tensor method reduces the force-calculation imbalance factor from 3.0 to 1.7 versus LAMMPS's native method. Near-perfect balance (imbalance factor close to 1.0) is achieved with LAMMPS recursive bisectioning on an irregular grid and ALL's histogram method on a staggered grid. Load balancing a staggered grid with ALL is significantly faster than bisectioning an irregular grid with LAMMPS, though per-timestep communication costs are lower for the irregular grid due to its lower surface-to-volume ratio.
AI.conclusion: The choice of load-balancing method strongly affects adaptive-precision EAM-ACE performance; ALL's modified tensor and histogram methods outperform LAMMPS native schemes in balance quality and rebalancing speed, while domain geometry trades rebalancing cost against communication cost. The authors additionally propose a strategy to identify the ideal load-balancing frequency for adaptive-precision simulations.

title: Fröhlich Bipolarons in Two-Dimensional Materials
summary: Motivated by the progress in the physics of two-dimensional materials and the recent two-dimensional generalization of the Fröhlich model, we study the formation of bipolarons in polar monolayers. Because of very special nonlocal dielectric screening in two dimensions, this setting differs qualitatively from the conventional Fröhlich model. In monolayers, (i) long wavelength LO phonons acquire a nontrivial dispersion; (ii) the Fröhlich electron-phonon vertex becomes momentum-dependent and regular at small momenta; and (iii) direct repulsion between charge carriers takes the Keldysh-Rytova form. Using the Feynman path-integral variational approach, we show that the region in the parameter space where stable bipolarons exist is strongly modified compared to the usual quasi-two-dimensional model with dispersionless phonons. Specifically, in the most favorable limit, when the ratio $σ_0$ of the static polarizability to the high-frequency polarizability tends to infinity, the lower critical coupling, sufficient for the formation of bipolarons, can be made arbitrarily small. More surprisingly, we demonstrate that no stable bipolarons can exist in the strong coupling limit: in the isolated monolayer the stability region is always confined to a finite range of coupling constants. In general, the stability region is strongly shifted toward large values of the polarizability ratio $σ_0$, well beyond the parameter regimes in representative crystals, which indicates that polar monolayers do not favor bipolarons.

AI.tldr: Bipolaron formation in polar monolayers is studied using the 2D Fröhlich model with nonlocal screening; the stability region is strongly modified, shifts to large polarizability ratios, and is confined to a finite coupling range with no stable bipolarons in the strong-coupling limit.
AI.motivation: Recent progress in 2D materials physics and the 2D generalization of the Fröhlich model motivate revisiting bipolaron formation, since nonlocal dielectric screening in 2D makes this setting qualitatively different from the conventional Fröhlich model and the usual quasi-2D description.
AI.method: The authors analyze the 2D Fröhlich model for polar monolayers, accounting for (i) nontrivial LO phonon dispersion at long wavelengths, (ii) a momentum-dependent, regular Fröhlich electron-phonon vertex at small momenta, and (iii) Keldysh-Rytova form of direct carrier-carrier repulsion. They apply the Feynman path-integral variational approach to determine bipolaron stability.
AI.result: The bipolaron stability region is strongly modified relative to the quasi-2D model with dispersionless phonons. In the most favorable limit (static-to-high-frequency polarizability ratio σ0 → ∞), the lower critical coupling for bipolaron formation becomes arbitrarily small. However, no stable bipolarons exist in the strong-coupling limit: in the isolated monolayer the stability region is confined to a finite range of coupling constants. The stability region is generally shifted toward large σ0, beyond regimes of representative crystals.
AI.conclusion: Polar monolayers do not favor bipolaron formation: their stability window is finite in coupling and requires polarizability ratios well beyond those of representative crystals.

title: Exact Nonlinear Active Microrheology in Diffusive Single-File Systems
summary: Active microrheology probes a crowded medium by forcing a tracer and measuring its response. In single-file transport, where particles cannot overtake, a constant force $F$ produces a subballistic displacement $\langle X_t\rangle\simeq \sqrt{t}\,ξ(F)$ together with a persistent bath deformation. Despite decades of work, the exact nonlinear response at arbitrary force has remained confined to a few special solvable models. Here we remove this restriction by combining recent advances in hydrodynamic transport coefficients, a pressure-balance formulation of the local drive, and single-file duality, which eliminates the resulting moving boundary. This yields a closed exact boundary-value problem for general diffusive single files, determining both $ξ(F)$ and the full density profile. For overdamped Brownian particles with general interactions, all microscopic interaction details enter only through the equilibrium equation of state, bringing realistic interacting systems, including finite-width quasi-one-dimensional channels, within exact reach. The solution also reveals universal global laws; in particular, the bath-density dipole is fixed by the applied force independently of the interaction potential.

AI.tldr: This work derives an exact solution for the nonlinear active microrheology response of general diffusive single-file systems at arbitrary force, showing subballistic displacement and that all interaction details enter only via the equilibrium equation of state.
AI.motivation: Active microrheology in crowded single-file media yields subballistic tracer displacement and persistent bath deformation, but the exact nonlinear response at arbitrary force has been limited to a few special solvable models, leaving realistic interacting systems out of reach.
AI.method: The authors combine recent advances in hydrodynamic transport coefficients, a pressure-balance formulation of the local drive, and single-file duality, which removes the resulting moving boundary, yielding a closed exact boundary-value problem for general diffusive single files.
AI.result: The framework determines both the subballistic amplitude ξ(F) and the full density profile. For overdamped Brownian particles with general interactions, microscopic interaction details enter only through the equilibrium equation of state, covering realistic interacting systems including finite-width quasi-one-dimensional channels. It also uncovers universal global laws, notably that the bath-density dipole is fixed by the applied force independently of the interaction potential.
AI.conclusion: The exact solution generalizes active microrheology of single files beyond special solvable models, establishing equation-of-state universality and interaction-independent global laws for arbitrary force.

title: Rapid Parameter Estimation from Photoluminescence Decays of Halide Perovskite Thin Films
comment: Main: 49 pages, 10 figures SI: 20 pages, 16 figures
summary: Extracting material parameters from experimental data is often challenging if no invertible analytical equation can be used to link the data with the quantities of interest. If the link between experiment and material parameters is given mathematically by a set of non-linear differential equations, these must be solved repeatedly during the traditional fitting procedure, resulting in long optimization times and limited insight into parameter uncertainty. Here, we present a parameter estimation workflow specifically aimed at transient photoluminescence measurements performed on lead-halide perovskite films. This workflow is accelerated using artificial neural networks for rapid comparison between experiment and simulation. An advantage of the method is the ability to rapidly scan multidimensional material parameter spaces and identify correlations between parameters that provide insights into the physics of non-radiative recombination in halide perovskites. Finally, we compare steady-state and transient photoluminescence and show how uncertainty in parameters such as the defect density can be reduced by including steady-state data in the parameter estimation workflow.

AI.tldr: An artificial-neural-network-accelerated workflow estimates material parameters from transient photoluminescence of lead-halide perovskite films, enabling rapid multidimensional parameter-space scanning, correlation analysis of non-radiative recombination, and uncertainty reduction when steady-state data are included.
AI.motivation: Extracting material parameters from experimental data is difficult when no invertible analytical relation links data to quantities of interest. When the experiment-to-parameter link is governed by non-linear differential equations, these must be solved repeatedly during traditional fitting, causing long optimization times and limited insight into parameter uncertainty.
AI.method: The authors present a parameter estimation workflow specifically for transient photoluminescence measurements on lead-halide perovskite films. Artificial neural networks are used to accelerate the comparison between experiment and simulation, replacing repeated numerical solution of the governing non-linear differential equations. The method enables rapid scanning of multidimensional material parameter spaces. Steady-state photoluminescence data are additionally incorporated into the workflow alongside transient data.
AI.result: The workflow enables rapid scanning of multidimensional material parameter spaces and identification of correlations between parameters, providing physical insight into non-radiative recombination in halide perovskites. Comparison of steady-state and transient photoluminescence shows that uncertainty in parameters such as defect density can be reduced by including steady-state data in the parameter estimation workflow.
AI.conclusion: Neural-network acceleration makes parameter estimation from transient photoluminescence tractable and interpretable, revealing parameter correlations relevant to non-radiative recombination. Adding steady-state photoluminescence data to the workflow reduces parameter uncertainty, e.g., for defect density.

title: LSR-Net: Learning the Forward Evolution Operator for Nonlinear Fluid Dynamics
summary: We introduce the Long-Short-Range Neural Network (LSR-Net), a novel neural operator architecture designed for data-driven forward evolution modeling, and extends it to the prediction of nonlinear fluid dynamics. LSR-Net learns the evolution operator of a dynamical system solely from pairs of initial and future state snapshots, which splits the learnable integral kernel into long-range (LR) and short-range (SR) components within stacked network blocks. While the SR component uses standard convolutions to capture local dynamics, the LR component employs a sum-of-exponentials (SOE) representation. This allows for the efficient computation of global interactions as a trainable Fourier multiplier, reducing computational complexity to $O(n \log n)$ where $n$ is the number of pixels in an input snapshot and requiring only a few parameters per channel. LSR-Net is evaluated on three challenging 2D benchmarks: the coupled Burgers equation, the wave equation with a spatially varying coefficient, and the nonlinear shallow water equation {(SWE)}. Results demonstrate that LSR-Net significantly outperforms the baseline short-range network (SR-Net) as well as FNO and DeepONets in predictive accuracy, achieving substantially lower relative errors by effectively capturing both local fine-scale structures and crucial global pattern interactions.

AI.tldr: LSR-Net is a neural operator that splits its learnable integral kernel into short-range (standard convolutions) and long-range (sum-of-exponentials Fourier multiplier) components, achieving O(n log n) complexity with few parameters and outperforming SR-Net, FNO, and DeepONets on three 2D fluid benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Data-driven forward evolution modeling of nonlinear fluid dynamics requires capturing both local fine-scale structures and global pattern interactions. Existing approaches (short-range networks, FNO, DeepONets) struggle to balance these multi-scale interactions efficiently, motivating an architecture that handles both regimes explicitly and at low computational cost.
AI.method: LSR-Net learns the evolution operator solely from pairs of initial and future state snapshots, without governing equations. Within stacked network blocks, the learnable integral kernel is decomposed into a short-range (SR) component implemented with standard convolutions for local dynamics, and a long-range (LR) component using a sum-of-exponentials (SOE) representation that computes global interactions as a trainable Fourier multiplier. This yields O(n log n) complexity (n = pixels per snapshot) with only a few parameters per channel.
AI.result: Evaluated on three challenging 2D benchmarks—the coupled Burgers equation, the wave equation with spatially varying coefficient, and the nonlinear shallow water equation (SWE)—LSR-Net significantly outperforms the baseline short-range network (SR-Net), FNO, and DeepONets in predictive accuracy, achieving substantially lower relative errors.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing the integral kernel into long- and short-range components enables efficient and accurate learning of nonlinear fluid dynamics, effectively capturing both local fine-scale structures and crucial global pattern interactions at reduced computational and parameter cost.

title: Chiral classical and quantum acoustics with hole-spin qubits
summary: Gate-defined hole spins combine strong spin-orbit coupling with exceptional strain sensitivity, making surface acoustic waves a natural route to remote, phase-coherent control. We show that counterpropagating surface acoustic waves can differ in coupling strength and in whether they predominantly drive spin rotations or modulate the qubit frequency. We call the transverse transition-strength imbalance spin-acoustic chirality and show that it is tunable through gate-controlled reshaping of the dot confinement. Combining a multiband Luttinger-Kohn Hamiltonian with the Bir-Pikus description of strain and 3D piezoelectric finite-element simulations, we obtain the acoustic g-matrix modulation governing coherent SAW driving. Quantizing the same strain-mediated interaction yields the corresponding single-phonon coupling, and a generalized anisotropic Rabi interaction with co-rotating, counter-rotating, and longitudinal components, linking classical chirality to quantum anisotropy and directional one-phonon emission. Magnetic field orientation and dot shape tune the acoustic chirality and operator selectivity. We illustrate this framework through bichromatic coherence protection and phonon-mediated heralded Bell-state initialization.

AI.tldr: Counterpropagating surface acoustic waves (SAWs) couple asymmetrically to gate-defined hole spins, an effect termed spin-acoustic chirality that is gate-tunable via dot confinement reshaping and controls directional single-phonon emission.
AI.motivation: Gate-defined hole spins have strong spin-orbit coupling and exceptional strain sensitivity, making SAWs attractive for remote, phase-coherent qubit control. However, the directional (counterpropagating) asymmetry of SAW-spin coupling and its microscopic origin and tunability were not established.
AI.method: Multiband Luttinger-Kohn Hamiltonian combined with Bir-Pikus strain description and 3D piezoelectric finite-element simulations yield the acoustic g-matrix modulation driving coherent SAW control. Quantizing the same strain-mediated interaction gives the single-phonon coupling and a generalized anisotropic Rabi interaction with co-rotating, counter-rotating, and longitudinal components.
AI.result: Counterpropagating SAWs differ in coupling strength and in whether they mainly drive spin rotations or modulate the qubit frequency; this transverse transition-strength imbalance (spin-acoustic chirality) is tunable by gate-controlled reshaping of the dot confinement. Magnetic field orientation and dot shape tune acoustic chirality and operator selectivity. Classical chirality links to quantum anisotropy and directional one-phonon emission.
AI.conclusion: The framework connects classical SAW chirality to quantum anisotropy and directional phonon emission, illustrated by bichromatic coherence protection and phonon-mediated heralded Bell-state initialization, providing a route to remote, phase-coherent hole-spin control.

title: Recent progress on thermal transport in one-dimensional long-range interacting Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou lattice systems
summary: Long-range (LR) interactions are no longer just a theoretical idea: they can be engineered in several low-dimensional platforms and offer a new way to control heat transport. At the same time, they push beyond the standard picture developed mainly for short-range, momentum-conserving lattices. In this review, we consider one-dimensional Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou (FPUT)-type lattices where LR effects enter mainly through a quartic anharmonic coupling that decays as a power law, characterized by an exponent σ. Our goal is to explain, in a unified way, how LR anharmonicity changes microscopic energy exchange, collective dynamics, and the macroscopic scaling laws of heat conduction-while also clarifying what is well established and what is still debated (For more details of the abstract, please see the main text and paper).

AI.tldr: This review unifies how long-range anharmonic interactions in one-dimensional FPUT-type lattices alter microscopic energy exchange, collective dynamics, and macroscopic heat-conduction scaling laws.
AI.motivation: Long-range (LR) interactions are now experimentally realizable in low-dimensional platforms and provide new routes to control heat transport. However, they challenge the standard framework of heat conduction developed for short-range, momentum-conserving lattices, creating a need for a coherent account of their effects.
AI.method: Review of one-dimensional Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou (FPUT)-type lattices in which LR effects enter primarily via a quartic anharmonic coupling that decays as a power law with exponent σ. The analysis links microscopic energy exchange, collective dynamics, and macroscopic heat-conduction scaling, distinguishing established results from open debates.
AI.result: The review synthesizes how LR anharmonicity modifies microscopic energy-exchange processes, collective vibrational dynamics, and the resulting macroscopic scaling laws of heat conduction in FPUT-type chains.
AI.conclusion: LR anharmonicity reshapes heat transport beyond the short-range paradigm; the review clarifies what is well established versus still contested, with detailed discussion deferred to the main text.

title: The role of disconnections in redox-induced phase transformation of metal oxides
comment: 7 pages and 4 figures in the main text; 10 pages and 6 figures in supporting information
summary: Detailed atomic-level understanding of the phase transformation between magnetite (${\rm Fe_3 O_4}$) and haematite (${\rm Fe_2 O_3}$) is lacking, despite widespread interest in redox reactions of metal oxide systems. While the magnetite-to-haematite transformation entails the addition of oxygen to the system and thus a net diffusive flux, haematite formations have been reported to grow along well-defined habits on the close-packed $\{0001\}_{\rm Fe_2 O_3}//\{111\}_{\rm Fe_3 O_4}$ planes. The propagation of the phase interface in the bulk is thus thought to maintain the oxygen sublattice fixed up to a shear, and to require long-range diffusion of iron ions. In this letter we propose interfacial steps with dislocation character, i.e. disconnections, as the elementary defects propagating the transformation. We use the topological model of interfacial defects to predict three disconnection modes for the system, and we employ scanning transmission electron microscopy to ascertain their presence in a haematite/magnetite interface of a partially oxidised magnetite powder. Using atomistic simulations, we determine the equilibrium structures of the disconnections, and study their motion and how they accomplish the transformation, obtaining excellent agreement with atomic-resolution experimental observations.

AI.tldr: This letter identifies interfacial disconnections as the elementary defects that propagate the magnetite-to-haematite phase transformation, predicting three modes via the topological model and confirming them experimentally with STEM and atomistic simulations.
AI.motivation: Despite broad interest in redox reactions of metal oxide systems, a detailed atomic-level understanding of the magnetite (Fe3O4) to haematite (Fe2O3) transformation is lacking. The transformation involves oxygen addition and net diffusive flux, yet haematite grows along well-defined habits on close-packed {0001}Fe2O3//{111}Fe3O4 planes, implying the oxygen sublattice remains fixed (up to a shear) while long-range iron diffusion occurs. The elementary defects controlling interface propagation in the bulk were unidentified.
AI.method: The authors apply the topological model of interfacial defects to predict disconnection modes for the Fe3O4/Fe2O3 system. They use scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) to identify these defects at a haematite/magnetite interface in a partially oxidised magnetite powder. Atomistic simulations are then used to determine the equilibrium structures of the disconnections and to study their motion and the mechanism by which they accomplish the transformation.
AI.result: The topological model predicts three disconnection modes. STEM observations ascertain their presence at the haematite/magnetite interface. Atomistic simulations yield equilibrium disconnection structures, and the simulated motion and transformation mechanism show excellent agreement with atomic-resolution experimental observations.
AI.conclusion: Interfacial disconnections with dislocation character are the elementary defects propagating the magnetite-to-haematite transformation. The combination of topological modelling, STEM, and atomistic simulation provides a consistent atomic-level description of the transformation, with simulated results in excellent agreement with experiment.

title: Layer-Dependent Vibrational and Optical Properties of $\mathrm{Mo}{0.58}\mathrm{W}{0.42}\mathrm{Se}_2$ Alloy
summary: Semiconducting Mo$_x$W$_{1-x}$Se$_2$ alloys provide a versatile platform for tailoring the optical properties of two-dimensional materials through both composition and layer thickness. Here, we systematically investigate mechanically exfoliated Mo$_{0.58}$W$_{0.42}$Se$_2$ flakes ranging from monolayer (1L) to nine layers by combining Raman scattering (RS), photoluminescence (PL), reflectance contrast (RC) spectroscopy, and first-principles phonon calculations. Thirteen RS peaks are identified, including the low-frequency interlayer shear mode, whose thickness dependence is well described by a linear-chain model, yielding an interlayer force constant of $K_s=(2.996\pm0.015)\times10^{19}$ N m$^{-3}$. PL measurements reveal a crossover from the direct-bandgap 1L to indirect-bandgap multilayers. The thickness evolution of the indirect optical transition is quantitatively reproduced using a quantum-confinement model, yielding an out-of-plane reduced effective mass of $μ_\perp=0.75 m_0$. RC spectroscopy reveals four excitonic resonances. While the A and B excitons associated with the $K^\pm$ valleys remain nearly independent of layer thickness, the higher-energy C and D resonances originating from the band-nesting regions exhibit pronounced redshifts, reflecting substantial thickness-induced modifications of the electronic band structure. These results establish comprehensive spectroscopic fingerprints of flake thickness, interlayer coupling, and electronic structure in Mo$_x$W$_{1-x}$Se$_2$ alloys and provide a reliable, non-destructive framework for their optical characterization.

AI.tldr: A combined RS, PL, RC, and DFT study of mechanically exfoliated Mo0.58W0.42Se2 flakes (1–9 layers) establishes comprehensive thickness-dependent spectroscopic fingerprints, quantifying interlayer coupling, bandgap crossover, and excitonic behavior in 2D alloy semiconductors.
AI.motivation: Mo_xW_{1-x}Se_2 alloys offer a tunable platform for engineering the optical properties of 2D materials via composition and layer thickness, but a systematic understanding of how thickness governs interlayer coupling, band structure, and excitonic resonances in these alloys is lacking.
AI.method: Mechanically exfoliated Mo0.58W0.42Se2 flakes from monolayer to nine layers were studied using resonant Raman scattering (RS), photoluminescence (PL), reflectance contrast (RC) spectroscopy, and first-principles phonon calculations. Thickness-dependent data were analyzed with a linear-chain model for interlayer shear modes and a quantum-confinement model for the indirect transition.
AI.result: Thirteen RS peaks were identified, including the low-frequency interlayer shear mode, whose thickness dependence yields an interlayer force constant of K_s = (2.996 ± 0.015) × 10^19 N m^-3. PL reveals a direct-to-indirect bandgap crossover from 1L to multilayers, quantitatively reproduced with an out-of-plane reduced effective mass of μ⊥ = 0.75 m0. RC spectroscopy resolves four excitonic resonances: A and B excitons (K± valleys) are nearly thickness-independent, while the higher-energy C and D resonances (band-nesting regions) exhibit pronounced redshifts due to thickness-induced band structure modifications.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish comprehensive spectroscopic fingerprints of flake thickness, interlayer coupling, and electronic structure in Mo_xW_{1-x}Se_2 alloys, providing a reliable non-destructive framework for their optical characterization.

title: A first introduction to Matrix Product State algorithms for the integration of Lindblad equation
summary: In this introductory review, we present and compare four algorithms for the numerical integration of the Lindblad equation for one-dimensional quantum lattice systems. All four methods are based on Matrix Product State representations and can be viewed as extensions of the Time-Evolving Block Decimation (TEBD) algorithm to open quantum systems. Two approaches directly integrate the vectorized Lindblad equation, one of them explicitly enforcing the positivity of the density matrix. The other two rely on stochastic unravelings of the Lindblad equation, namely the quantum trajectory and quantum state diffusion approaches. We discuss the principles, numerical implementation, accuracy, and computational efficiency of the different methods, and benchmark them against an exactly solvable free fermion model.

AI.tldr: Introductory review comparing four MPS-based numerical methods for integrating the Lindblad equation in 1D quantum lattice systems, benchmarked against an exactly solvable free fermion model.
AI.motivation: Numerical simulation of open quantum systems in one dimension requires efficient methods capable of handling the Lindblad master equation, motivating a comparative review of available MPS-based approaches.
AI.method: Four algorithms extending TEBD to open quantum systems are presented: (1) direct integration of the vectorized Lindblad equation, (2) a variant explicitly enforcing density matrix positivity, (3) the quantum trajectory (stochastic unraveling) approach, and (4) quantum state diffusion. All use Matrix Product State representations.
AI.result: The methods are benchmarked against an exactly solvable free fermion model, with discussion of their principles, numerical implementation, accuracy, and computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The review provides a comparative assessment of the practical trade-offs among MPS/TEBD-based approaches for open-system dynamics, guiding method selection based on accuracy and efficiency requirements.

title: A Pseudoscalar Representation Mapping from Parent-Group Vibrational Normal Modes to Symmetry-Adapted Magnetic Structures
summary: Conventional approaches classify symmetry-allowed magnetic configurations but do not by themselves establish a direct, mode-resolved correspondence with parent-lattice vibrations. Here, we formulate a universal determinant-induced pseudoscalar twist for all 32 crystallographic point groups, establishing an exact representation-to-geometry correspondence between parent vibrations and magnetic order. Within the paramagnetic gray group $G\timesΘ_{\mathcal{T}}$, the spatial twist determines symmetry-defined magnetic geometry, while time-reversal parity independently specifies magnetic character. Each parent phonon irrep $Γ$ maps to $Γ_{\mathrm{mag}}=Γ\otimesΓ_{\mathrm{ps}}$, preserving multiplicities and yielding the projection identity $P_{\mathrm{mag},mn}^{(Γ\otimesΓ_{\mathrm{ps}})}=P_{\mathrm{ph},mn}^{(Γ)}$ under the common Cartesian realization. This establishes the \textit{Template Principle}: parent vibrational modes furnish real-space templates whose symmetry-enforced nodal manifolds are inherited exactly. Applied to monolayer $\mathrm{Cd}_2\mathrm{N}_3$, the framework identifies the ferrimagnetic ground state from the parent $A_{2u}$ sector, confirmed by first-principles calculations, alongside cluster magnetic octupoles and antiferromagnetic manifolds. It further provides an \textit{a priori} parent-group criterion for screening symmetry-allowed linear magnetic responses.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates a determinant-induced pseudoscalar twist that establishes an exact mode-resolved correspondence between parent-lattice vibrations and symmetry-allowed magnetic configurations across all 32 crystallographic point groups, and applies it to monolayer Cd2N3.
AI.motivation: Conventional approaches classify symmetry-allowed magnetic configurations but do not by themselves establish a direct, mode-resolved correspondence with parent-lattice vibrations. The authors aim to bridge this gap by linking parent vibrations to magnetic order geometrically.
AI.method: They introduce a universal determinant-induced pseudoscalar twist Γ_ps for all 32 crystallographic point groups. Within the paramagnetic gray group G×Θ_T, the spatial twist determines symmetry-defined magnetic geometry while time-reversal parity specifies magnetic character. Each parent phonon irrep Γ maps to Γ_mag = Γ⊗Γ_ps, preserving multiplicities and yielding the projection identity P_mag,mn^(Γ⊗Γ_ps) = P_ph,mn^(Γ) under the common Cartesian realization. This defines a Template Principle. The framework is applied to monolayer Cd2N3 and cross-checked with first-principles calculations.
AI.result: For monolayer Cd2N3, the framework identifies the ferrimagnetic ground state originating from the parent A2u sector, confirmed by first-principles calculations, along with cluster magnetic octupoles and antiferromagnetic manifolds.
AI.conclusion: The Template Principle shows that parent vibrational modes furnish real-space templates whose symmetry-enforced nodal manifolds are inherited exactly by magnetic order. The framework also provides an a priori parent-group criterion for screening symmetry-allowed linear magnetic responses.

title: Synthetic twist geometry in mesoscopic quantum circuits: geometric capacitance and chiral mode splitting
summary: We propose a route for encoding a helicoidally twisted synthetic geometry in mesoscopic quantum circuits. A torsionless spatial metric with twist parameter $\Om$ defines an electrostatic capacitance kernel whose angular--axial sector contains the chiral coupling $-2\Om mk$. We show that this kernel can be implemented by a finite, quantizable circuit graph built only from positive two-node capacitors: diagonal bridges generate the cross term, and the dimensionless twist is the ratio of diagonal to total angular capacitance. The resulting capacitance matrix enters the Hamiltonian through $C^{-1}(\etaT)$ and splits counter-rotating synthetic modes. Exact finite-graph diagonalization confirms the analytic spectrum and shows that closed longitudinal circulation is required; with open boundaries the bridge phase is gauge removable and the doublets remain degenerate. Simulated spectroscopy resolves the chiral fan, while disorder simulations indicate that calibrated percent-level reactive disorder does not obscure the deterministic splitting in the parameter range considered. Twist textures produce interface modes, Josephson nonlinearities make the Kerr sector chirality dependent, and the same doublet provides a detuning knob for non-Hermitian exceptional-point control. For representative circuit-QED parameters the splitting is in the tens-of-MHz range, well above typical resonator linewidths.

AI.tldr: A helicoidal twist is encoded into mesoscopic quantum circuits via an electrostatic capacitance kernel with a chiral coupling term, implemented by a quantizable capacitor graph that produces measurable synthetic-mode splitting.
AI.motivation: The paper seeks a route to realize helicoidal (twisted) synthetic geometry in mesoscopic quantum circuits, aiming to encode a spatial metric with a twist parameter into circuit degrees of freedom and thereby engineer chirality-dependent quantum behavior.
AI.method: A torsionless spatial metric with twist parameter Omega is used to define an electrostatic capacitance kernel whose angular-axial sector contains the chiral coupling -2 Omega m k. This kernel is implemented through a finite, quantizable circuit graph built only from positive two-node capacitors: diagonal bridges generate the cross term, and the dimensionless twist equals the ratio of diagonal to total angular capacitance. The capacitance matrix enters the Hamiltonian via C^{-1}(eta), and the resulting chiral fan is studied by exact finite-graph diagonalization, simulated spectroscopy, and disorder simulations.
AI.result: Exact finite-graph diagonalization confirms the analytic spectrum and shows that closed longitudinal circulation is required for the splitting; with open boundaries the bridge phase is gauge removable and the doublets remain degenerate. Simulated spectroscopy resolves the chiral fan. Calibrated percent-level reactive disorder does not obscure the deterministic splitting in the parameter range considered. Twist textures produce interface modes, Josephson nonlinearities make the Kerr sector chirality dependent, and the doublet provides a detuning knob for non-Hermitian exceptional-point control. For representative circuit-QED parameters, the splitting is in the tens-of-MHz range, well above typical resonator linewidths.
AI.conclusion: Helicoidal twisted synthetic geometry can be realized in mesoscopic quantum circuits using simple positive capacitors, yielding a chiral mode splitting that is robust to moderate reactive disorder and experimentally resolvable within circuit-QED parameters.

title: Current fluctuations of diffusive systems with a battery
summary: For a diffusive system on a ring, with a battery at the origin, we use the macroscopic fluctuation theory (MFT) to obtain the large deviation function of the current. In the case of non-interacting particles, the predictions of the MFT agree with the result of a direct exact microscopic calculation. To our surprise, the large deviation function of non-interacting particles with a battery has the same form as for the Symmetric Simple Exclusion Process (SSEP) with open boundary conditions. For the SSEP on a ring with a battery, the predictions of the MFT seem to agree with the results of long Monte Carlo simulations, although much longer simulations would be needed to better test the validity of these predictions.

AI.tldr: Using macroscopic fluctuation theory (MFT), the authors compute the large deviation function (LDF) of the current in a diffusive ring driven by a battery at the origin, finding an unexpected equivalence between non-interacting particles and the SSEP.
AI.motivation: The paper seeks to characterize current fluctuations in a diffusive ring geometry with a battery at the origin, extending fluctuation statistics beyond standard open-boundary setups and probing whether MFT remains valid when particle interactions and driving are combined.
AI.method: The large deviation function of the current is derived within the macroscopic fluctuation theory for a diffusive system on a ring with a battery at the origin. For non-interacting particles, the MFT prediction is benchmarked against a direct exact microscopic calculation. For the SSEP on a ring with a battery, MFT predictions are compared with long Monte Carlo simulations.
AI.result: For non-interacting particles, the MFT prediction agrees with the exact microscopic result. Notably, their LDF with a battery takes the same form as that of the SSEP with open boundary conditions. For the SSEP on a ring with a battery, MFT predictions appear consistent with long Monte Carlo simulations, though even longer runs are required for a definitive test.
AI.conclusion: MFT successfully captures current large deviations in a battery-driven diffusive ring, and the coincidence of the non-interacting battery case with the open-boundary SSEP LDF hints at a broader universality of current fluctuation statistics. Further numerical work is needed to firmly validate the SSEP ring-with-battery predictions.

title: Thermally Desorbable InN Capping Layers for Nitride Surface Science
summary: Group III-nitride thin films are essential for optoelectronic and power devices, where surface and interface quality critically influence performance. It is often necessary to transfer these films through atmosphere for processing or characterization steps, which can introduce significant surface contamination. Here we demonstrate a technique to protect the surface of III-N films during atmospheric exposure by capping with sacrificial InN layers. Using molecular beam epitaxy grown AlGaN films as our representative protected material, we take advantage of the lower decomposition and desorption temperatures of InN and metallic In to remove the protective cap layer in situ via thermal desorption without damaging the AlGaN film beneath. Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) measurements of the valence band dispersion in Al0.4Ga0.6N demonstrate that the film surface is recovered after InN decapping, highlighting the versatility of this process in allowing further surface-sensitive characterization of films that had been exposed to air.

AI.tldr: A sacrificial InN cap layer protects III-nitride film surfaces during atmospheric exposure and is removed in situ by thermal desorption, fully recovering the AlGaN surface as confirmed by ARPES.
AI.motivation: Group III-nitride thin films are critical for optoelectronic and power devices, and their performance depends strongly on surface and interface quality. However, transferring these films through atmosphere for processing or characterization introduces significant surface contamination, so an effective protection strategy is needed.
AI.method: Molecular beam epitaxy (MBE)-grown AlGaN films were capped with sacrificial InN layers. Exploiting the lower decomposition and desorption temperatures of InN and metallic In, the cap was removed in situ by thermal desorption without damaging the underlying AlGaN. Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) was used to assess the valence band dispersion of Al0.4Ga0.6N after decapping.
AI.result: ARPES measurements of the valence band dispersion in Al0.4Ga0.6N show that the film surface is recovered after InN decapping, even though the films had been exposed to air.
AI.conclusion: Sacrificial InN capping combined with in-situ thermal decapping is a versatile approach for protecting III-N film surfaces during atmospheric exposure, enabling subsequent surface-sensitive characterization of transferred films.

title: Hierarchy of time scales in kinetically constrained models via stochastic-generator expansion
summary: We revisit the hierarchy of relaxation time scales in stochastic kinetically constrained models (KCMs) obeying detailed balance, using an expansion method developed recently for their quantum counterparts. In the classical setting, we expand the stochastic generator in the low-temperature equilibrium concentration of excitations. As in quantum KCMs, successive truncations of the expansion reveal a nested hierarchy of metastable configurations that remain frozen on progressively longer time scales. Applying the method to the high-to-low temperature quench in the classical one-dimensional East and Fredrickson-Andersen models, we recover the known hierarchy of metastable plateaus and the associated perturbative time scales. We find that the hierarchical time scales are related to the smallest domain lengths. Our results show that the method developed for quantum kinetically constrained models can be used to provide a systematic description of slow relaxation in their classical counterparts as well.

AI.tldr: The authors apply a low-temperature expansion method, originally developed for quantum kinetically constrained models (KCMs), to classical stochastic KCMs with detailed balance, revealing a nested hierarchy of metastable configurations and relaxation time scales.
AI.motivation: Understanding the hierarchy of relaxation time scales in stochastic kinetically constrained models is important for describing slow relaxation and glassy dynamics. The paper aims to transfer a recently developed expansion method from quantum KCMs to the classical setting to provide a systematic description of slow relaxation.
AI.method: The stochastic generator is expanded in the low-temperature equilibrium concentration of excitations. Successive truncations of this expansion are analyzed for the classical one-dimensional East and Fredrickson-Andersen models under a high-to-low temperature quench.
AI.result: The expansion recovers the known hierarchy of metastable plateaus and associated perturbative time scales. The hierarchical time scales are found to be related to the smallest domain lengths.
AI.conclusion: The method developed for quantum kinetically constrained models can also systematically describe slow relaxation in classical KCMs, demonstrating its broader applicability.

title: ERAF4XRD: A multimodal agentic framework for constructing validated experimental X-ray diffraction databases from scientific literature
summary: The scientific literature contains decades of experimental measurements that remain difficult to access as structured data for modern AI and data-driven research. Much of this information is distributed across figures, captions, text, and tables, requiring experimental data and their context to be identified, connected, and verified before they can be reused. Here we introduce ERAF4XRD (Experiment Reader Agentic Framework for X-Ray Diffraction), a fully automated multimodal (i.e., image and text), multi-agent framework that reconstructs validated X-ray diffraction (XRD) records from scientific publications. ERAF4XRD downloads and screens documents, identifies XRD figures, extracts and links metadata to the corresponding experimental data, and validates outputs against source evidence using an independent validation agent. On a manually curated benchmark of 273 scientific publications containing 3,150 candidate figures, ERAF4XRD achieved up to 98.7% accuracy for XRD figure identification and generated 1,400 metadata values across 22 fields. Independent manual assessment of the final validated records yielded 98.5% precision and 90.7% recall, with no unsupported metadata observed among 443 evaluated fields. By moving beyond information extraction to the reconstruction and validation of linked experimental records, ERAF4XRD establishes an automated approach for transforming published scientific information into machine-readable experimental datasets for AI and data-driven science.

AI.tldr: ERAF4XRD is a fully automated multimodal multi-agent framework that reconstructs validated, machine-readable X-ray diffraction records from scientific publications, achieving high accuracy in figure identification and metadata extraction with independent validation.
AI.motivation: Decades of experimental measurements in the scientific literature remain inaccessible as structured data because information is scattered across figures, captions, text, and tables, requiring labor-intensive identification, linking, and verification before reuse for modern AI and data-driven research.
AI.method: ERAF4XRD (Experiment Reader Agentic Framework for X-Ray Diffraction) is a fully automated multimodal (image and text) multi-agent framework. It downloads and screens documents, identifies XRD figures, extracts and links metadata to corresponding experimental data, and validates outputs against source evidence using an independent validation agent. Evaluated on a manually curated benchmark of 273 publications with 3,150 candidate figures.
AI.result: Achieved up to 98.7% accuracy for XRD figure identification and generated 1,400 metadata values across 22 fields. Independent manual assessment of final validated records yielded 98.5% precision and 90.7% recall, with no unsupported metadata observed among 443 evaluated fields.
AI.conclusion: By moving beyond information extraction to the reconstruction and validation of linked experimental records, ERAF4XRD establishes an automated approach for transforming published scientific information into machine-readable experimental datasets for AI and data-driven science.

title: A microscopic heat engine with many hidden variables
summary: Microscopic motors are commonly monitored through a single mechanical coordinate, whereas the chemical, conformational, or rotational cycles that sustain their motion remain unresolved. Mechanical stall is defined by the vanishing of the mean observed velocity; this scalar condition, however, does not generally imply thermodynamic reversibility. We analyze an overdamped Brownian motor in which one observed coordinate is coupled to several internal phases through a single shared interaction potential. Because the transmitted force and the reaction torques derive from the same energy, the resulting rank-one reciprocal structure yields an exact pointwise identity between the observed and hidden probability currents. This identity provides an exact expression for the entropy production at stall for an arbitrary periodic interaction. In particular, a positive current-square dissipation in the mechanical channel, defined from the full stationary state through the coupling-coordinate-resolved local velocity, determines together with the stall load the collective hidden current projected onto the coupling direction. The stationary one-coordinate marginal current nevertheless vanishes identically at stall; consequently, the stationary marginal density and mean displacement current do not determine this dissipation. Hidden currents orthogonal to the coupling direction dissipate without affecting the observed motion and generate an irreducible contribution that cannot be inferred from the rank-one mechanical channel.
